modules.title: Why Git Exists
modules.summary: What version control is, the problem it solves, and how Git thinks about your files.

body.p: Imagine you're writing an essay. You save it as `essay.docx`. Then you make big changes, get nervous, and save a copy: `essay_v2.docx`. Then `essay_v2_final.docx`. Then `essay_v2_final_REALLY_FINAL.docx`. Two weeks later you have eleven files, you don't remember which one has the good introduction, and you just overwrote the only copy that had it.
Every programmer, writer, and designer has lived this. The problem isn't you — it's that files only remember their **latest** state. The moment you save, the past is gone.

body.h: Version control: a time machine for your project

body.p: A *version control system* (VCS) fixes this by recording **snapshots** of your whole project over time. Think of it like save points in a video game: at any moment you can say "save my progress here," and later you can go back to any save point, compare them, or branch off in a new direction — without losing anything.

body.analogy: A Git repository is like a photo album of your project. Each snapshot (called a **commit**) is a photo of every file at one moment, with a caption saying what changed and why. The album never forgets a photo.

body.p: Git is the world's most widely used version control system. It was created in 2005 by Linus Torvalds (the creator of Linux) and today it runs almost every software project you've heard of — and plenty of non-software ones too: books, research papers, legal documents, game assets.
Three ideas to hold onto — we'll return to them constantly:

list: A **repository** ("repo") is your project folder plus its entire recorded history.
A **commit** is one snapshot of the project, with a message describing it.
The **history** is the chain of commits — you can walk back through it any time.

body.tip: You don't need to be a programmer to use Git. If you can make files and type a few commands, you can use Git. This course assumes zero prior knowledge.

lessons.title: How Git thinks: snapshots, not saves

body.p: Before you type a single command, it helps to see the mental model. Git splits your project into **three areas**:

list: The **working directory** — your actual files, the ones you edit. Just a normal folder.
The **staging area** — a waiting room where you gather the changes you want in your next snapshot.
The **repository** — the album of permanent snapshots (commits).

body.analogy: Picture a photographer's studio. The **working directory** is the messy room where things happen. The **staging area** is the spot in front of the camera — you deliberately arrange what should be in the photo. The **commit** is pressing the shutter: click, that arrangement is recorded forever.

body.p: Every commit remembers which commit came before it. That link is what turns individual snapshots into a **history** you can travel along. Here's what a young project's history looks like — three commits, oldest on the left:

graph.caption: Three commits on the main branch. The label 'main' points at the newest commit; HEAD means 'you are here'.

body.p: In this course, that diagram is live: it redraws itself after every command you run, so you can *watch* your history grow. That picture — dots connected by lines — is the single most important thing to understand about Git. Everything else (branches, merges, undoing mistakes) is just moving around on it.

body.tip: Reassurance up front: once something is committed in Git, it is very hard to lose. Most "disasters" beginners fear are recoverable. We'll even practice recovering from them in Module 9.

lessons.title: init: putting a folder under Git's protection

body.p: A Git repository starts life as a completely ordinary folder. The command `git init` (short for *initialize*) turns it into a repository. What actually happens is delightfully simple: Git creates one hidden subfolder called `.git`, and that's where it will keep every snapshot, forever.

body.analogy: `git init` is like installing a filing cabinet in the corner of your office. Your desk (the working directory) looks exactly the same afterward — but now there's a place where copies of your work can be stored safely and organized by date.

body.code:
git init
# → Initialized empty Git repository in /home/learner/project/.git/

body.p: Here's the part that surprises everyone: after `git init`, Git is **not** watching your files yet. It knows the folder exists, but every file in it is *untracked* — Git sees it, shrugs, and does nothing until you explicitly say "this file matters, include it in snapshots."
This is deliberate. Real projects contain junk that should never be in history (temporary files, passwords, huge downloads). Git makes you opt files **in**, never the other way around.

`git status` answers the question you'll ask a hundred times a day: *"Git, what do you see right now?"* It lists which files are untracked, which have changes, and which are staged for the next snapshot. It never changes anything — it's completely safe to run at any moment. When in doubt, `git status`.

body.tip: Get in the habit now: run `git status` before and after every other Git command until reading it feels boring. Boring is the goal.

body.p: You have a folder with a recipe file in it. Let's put it under version control and take the first snapshot. Watch the panels on the right as you go — you'll see files move between areas, and the graph gain its first dot.

modules.title: Staging vs Committing
modules.summary: Why the two-step save exists, how to craft precise commits, and how to un-stage when you change your mind.

lessons.title: The staging area: arrange, then shoot

body.p: Beginners often ask: why the two-step dance? Why `add` *and then* `commit` — why doesn't commit just save everything?

Because **a commit should tell one story**. Real work is messy: in one sitting you might fix a bug, rename a heading, and start a new feature. If commits were automatic "save everything" snapshots, each one would be a junk drawer of unrelated changes — and the history would be useless for answering "when did we fix that bug?" or "can we undo just the heading change?"

body.analogy: Back to the photographer's studio. Your working directory is the whole messy room. The **staging area** is the space in front of the camera. Before pressing the shutter you *choose* what's in frame: this change yes, that change not yet. `git add` places a change in frame. `git commit` clicks the shutter. The photo shows only what you staged.

body.h: The three areas, one more time

body.code:
working directory  --git add-->  staging area  --git commit-->  repository
   (your edits)                (next snapshot)               (permanent history)

body.p: Two crucial details beginners miss:

list: `git add` stages the file's contents **as they are right now**. If you edit the file again afterward, the *new* edits are not staged — the file shows up as both 'staged' and 'modified' at once. Not a bug: the frame holds the version you placed there.
Changed your mind? `git restore --staged <file>` takes a file back **out** of the frame without touching your actual edits. Nothing is lost — it just won't be in the next photo.

body.h: Seeing what's about to be committed

body.p: `git diff` shows edits you have **not** staged yet (working directory vs staging area). `git diff --staged` shows exactly what **will** go into the next commit (staging area vs last commit). Reading `git diff --staged` before committing is the closest thing Git has to a preview button.

body.tip: A good commit is like a good sentence: one idea. "Fix login typo" and "Add dark mode" should be two commits, even if you did them in the same hour. Your future self, hunting a bug at midnight, will thank you.

body.p: You're working on a tiny website that's already under version control. You've just edited **both** files — two unrelated changes. A lazy person would commit them together. You're going to split them like a pro, and practice un-staging along the way.

steps.say: Start with the compass. Both files show as **modified** — changed since the last commit, but nothing staged yet.
Stage **only** the headline change. The CSS change stays out of frame.
steps.hint: Type: git add index.html — just that one file, not a dot.

steps.say: Status now shows the split brain: index.html under 'Changes to be committed', style.css under 'Changes not staged'. Same folder, two different areas.
Preview exactly what the next commit will contain:
steps.hint: Type: git diff --staged — lines starting with - are removed, + are added.

steps.say: Commit it. Note the stat line: **1 file changed** — the CSS edit is untouched, still waiting in your working directory.
Now practice changing your mind. Stage the CSS file...
...and immediately un-stage it. Your edit is still in the file — check the panels — it's just out of the frame again. This is the safety valve you'll reach for constantly.
Finish the job: stage the CSS change again and commit it with its own message. Two changes, two commits, each telling one story.
steps.cmd:
git add style.css
git commit -m "Hot pink headline"
steps.hint: git add style.css, then git commit -m "Hot pink headline"

body.p: A realistic mess: you've modified two tracked files **and** created a brand-new one. Your job is to turn the mess into a tidy history. The checklist validates the final *shape of your history* — how you get there is up to you.

modules.title: Status & Diff: Reading What Changed
modules.summary: Read git status like a report instead of a wall of text, and learn the diff format you will meet in every code review for the rest of your life.

lessons.title: Anatomy of git status — and of a diff

body.p: You have typed `git status` a dozen times by now, and if you are like most beginners you have been skimming it. Every line of it is a precise answer to a precise question, and learning to read it — along with a diff — is most of what separates someone who *uses* Git from someone who is *nervous around* Git.

body.h: Status is a report with three shelves

body.p: `git status` sorts the interesting files in your project into three sections, ordered by how close they are to being in your next commit. The top two are areas you already know from Module 3 — the staging area first, then the working directory. The third is for files Git has never been asked to record at all.

body.analogy: Picture packing for a trip. **Changes to be committed** are the clothes already zipped into the suitcase. **Changes not staged for commit** are the clothes lying on the bed — chosen, but not packed. **Untracked files** are still in the wardrobe: Git has never packed them, doesn't know you want them, and will leave without them.

body.p: All three sections at once. Read it slowly:

body.code:
On branch main

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
	modified:   README.md

Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
	modified:   todo.txt

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	scratch.txt

list: `On branch main` — where you are working. (Branches arrive in Module 5.)
**Changes to be committed** — the staging area. `README.md` is in the suitcase: commit now and this is what you get.
**Changes not staged for commit** — the working directory. `todo.txt` has edits Git can see but was never asked to pack.
**Untracked files** — `scratch.txt` is brand new. Git has never stored a version of it and will not put it in any commit until you `git add` it.
The lines in parentheses are the exact commands Git suggests for each section — but read them before you run them: one of them is not like the others.

body.warn: Two of those suggestions are safe: `git add` and `git restore --staged <file>` only move a change between shelves. `git restore <file>` — same word, no `--staged` — throws your edit away and puts the file back to the last version Git knows about. There is no undo for that, because Git never had a copy of what you deleted. Check for the `--staged` before you press Enter.

body.p: A file can appear in **two** sections at once. Stage it, then edit it again: the suitcase holds the shirt you packed, and the bed holds the newer version you have ironed since. (Module 3’s camera, if you prefer: the frame still holds the version you placed in it.)

body.h: The line that trips absolutely everybody up

body.p: Now take `README.md` back out of the suitcase and ask again. Both files sit under **Changes not staged for commit**, and Git signs off with a line that reads like a contradiction:

body.code: no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")

body.p: It means: *"if you ran `git commit` this second, the commit would be empty."* **Changed is not the same as staged.** The clothes are all over the bed; the suitcase is empty. That line has confused more beginners than anything else Git prints.

body.tip: `git status` changes nothing. Ever. It is the one Git command you can run as often as you breathe, and the fastest way out of "what state am I in?"

body.h: A diff is a set of edit instructions

body.p: Status tells you *which* files changed, never *how*. That is `git diff`, and what it prints is a **unified diff** — the format used by every code-review tool, and by every programmer showing another what they changed. Learn it once, read it forever.

body.analogy: A diff is not a picture of the new file. It is a proofreader's marks on the old one: *cross out this line, write this one instead, and add that one at the end.* The unmarked lines are printed too, quietly, only so you can tell where on the page you are.

body.p: Here is the diff of that `todo.txt` edit:

body.code:
diff --git a/todo.txt b/todo.txt
index 88c4e99..525fdba 100644
--- a/todo.txt
+++ b/todo.txt
@@ -1,4 +1,5 @@
 - book the train
-- pack chargers
+- pack chargers (2x USB-C)
 - print tickets
 - water the plants
+- ask Sam to feed the cat

body.p: A header block, then the lines. Every part of it, once, so that none of it is ever mysterious again:

list: `diff --git a/todo.txt b/todo.txt` — the header. **a/** is the *before* version, **b/** the *after*: same file, two moments in time.
`index 88c4e99..525fdba 100644` — internal ids and file permissions. Ignore this line for the rest of your career.
`--- a/todo.txt` and `+++ b/todo.txt` — which side is before (`---`) and which is after (`+++`).

`@@ -1,4 +1,5 @@` — a **hunk header**, and the only cryptic part. Read it as: *the before side contributes 4 lines starting at line 1; the after side contributes 5.* A **hunk** is one neighbourhood of edits plus three lines of context either side, so edits in two far-apart places print as two `@@` blocks with the untouched middle left out.

In real Git there is often text *after* the closing `@@`, like `@@ -40,7 +40,9 @@ def process_order(order):`. That is not part of the numbers — it is Git quoting the nearest heading above the hunk, so you can see where you are. This sandbox leaves it off.

Then the lines themselves: `-` was **removed**, `+` was **added**, a leading **space** is unchanged **context**. A reworded line shows up as a `-` and a `+` together, because Git compares whole lines, never words.

body.tip: Mnemonic: `-` is what **left**, `+` is what **arrived**. Changing one word in a sentence therefore costs you a whole `-` line and a whole `+` line.

body.h: The real question: which two things is it comparing?

body.p: This is where people quietly get lost, and it is the heart of the module. `git diff` has no single meaning: it has a *pair of endpoints*, and the flag you use chooses them. Your file can live in three places — the last commit, the staging area, your working directory — so there are three interesting gaps between them. (`HEAD` is Git’s name for the commit you are sitting on right now.)

body.analogy: Back to the suitcase. `git diff` holds the bed up against the suitcase: *what have I chosen but not packed?* `git diff --staged` holds the suitcase up against the packing list you filed last trip: *what will this trip's list say?* And `git diff HEAD` ignores the suitcase entirely, comparing the whole room against that list.

body.p: Each row of the table reads older on the left, newer on the right — the direction `add` and `commit` push your work into history, which is why the last commit sits at the far left:

body.code:
git diff            staging area -> working directory
git diff --staged   last commit  -> staging area
git diff HEAD       last commit  -> working directory
git diff <A> <B>    commit A     -> commit B

body.tip: `git diff --cached` in older tutorials and answers online is the same command — `--cached` and `--staged` are two names for one flag. Both work everywhere, including here.

body.p: There is no such thing as *the* diff. Ask two of those questions in the same second, about the same repository, and you can get two completely different answers — both correct.

body.warn: Every form of `git diff` is blind to **untracked** files. `scratch.txt` appears in no diff at all, because Git has no earlier version of it to compare against. It becomes visible — to `git diff --staged` — once you `git add` it, and then it arrives as `new file mode` over `--- /dev/null` (Git saying "before, there was nothing") with every line prefixed `+`.

body.h: Looking backwards: one commit, or the gap between two

body.p: Everything so far compares the present against something. You can also point Git at the past — at one commit alone, or at the gap between two.

graph.caption: Four commits. `git show <ref>` opens one dot and prints what it changed. `git diff <A> <B>` measures the distance between two dots — it does not care how many commits sit in between.

- book the train
- print tickets
- pack chargers
A tiny offline app for planning trips.

list: `git show HEAD` — the newest commit: id, author, date, message, **and** the full diff of what it changed. Plain `git show` means the same thing.

`git show HEAD~1` — one commit further back; `HEAD~2` is two back. You can also paste a short id from `git log --oneline` — the history you met in Module 2, squeezed to one line per commit: short id, then message.
`git diff HEAD~3 HEAD` — the net change across the last three commits as one diff. The steps in between disappear; you see only before and after.

body.p: `status`, `diff`, `show` and `log` are all **read-only**. None of them can lose an edit or change what you are about to commit. Prod at them as much as you like — that is the entire point of this module.

A café keeps its menu in Git. Someone edited `menu.txt` since the last commit and left a scratch file lying around, and nobody wrote down what they changed. You are going to find out — reading before you touch anything, then staging and committing once you know what you are agreeing to.
Watch for the moment in the middle where a change **vanishes** from `git diff`. That disappearance is the most useful thing in this module.

steps.say: Last move: look backwards. `git diff HEAD~1 HEAD` asks for the *distance between two dots* — the commit before yours, and yours. Then open the commit itself: `git show` prints it from the inside, with its message, author and date above the very same diff. Run both and compare — the diff bodies are identical, and the only difference is the commit header on top.

git show

body.p: The pancake recipe has been through four commits and it no longer works — the pancakes come out flat. Nobody remembers editing anything they should not have.

Here is the thing about a good history: **every commit message is a promise about what that commit did.** Somewhere in these four commits, one of them quietly did something extra that its message never mentions. Find it with `git log`, `git show` and `git diff`, then undo only that.

`git diff HEAD~3 HEAD` compares the very first commit with the current one. Every difference in that diff should be explained by one of the four messages — except one. Look for a `-` line nobody promised.
To fix it, put the missing ingredient line back into the file (`echo "- 1 tsp baking powder" >> recipe.txt` works fine), then `git add recipe.txt` and `git commit -m "..."`.

list: `git status` is a report with three shelves: **staged** (in the suitcase), **not staged** (on the bed), **untracked** (still in the wardrobe).
**no changes added to commit** means "committing right now would produce an empty commit". Changed is not staged.
A diff is a list of edit instructions: `-` left, `+` arrived, a leading space is unchanged context, and `@@ -1,4 +1,5 @@` tells you where in the file you are.
`git diff` never has one meaning — always ask *which two endpoints?*
`git show <ref>` opens a single commit; `git diff <A> <B>` measures the gap between two.
Untracked files are invisible to every form of `git diff` until you `git add` them.
`status`, `diff`, `show` and `log` are read-only — none of them can hurt you. The one command on this page that can is `git restore <file>` without `--staged`: it discards your edit for good.

git diff --staged   last commit  -> staging area
git diff HEAD       last commit  -> working directory
git diff <A> <B>    commit A     -> commit B

graph.caption: A history you can now interrogate: `git show` any dot, `git diff` between any two.

modules.title: Branching
modules.summary: A branch is a sticky note pointing at one commit. How to make one, move between them, and keep two versions of your project alive at the same time.

lessons.title: A branch is a sticky note

body.p: Here is a situation every beginner meets. Your project works. You want to try something that might *not* work — a redesign, a rewrite, a wild idea you're only half sure about. The instinct is to duplicate the folder: `project` and `project-experiment`. And you are right back in `essay_v2_final_REALLY_FINAL` territory, except now you have two folders to keep in step with each other.

Git's answer is the **branch**. It is the most important idea in this course, and also the one most beginners get wrong — because the word sounds like it means "a copy of everything". It doesn't. Not even slightly.

Every commit has a unique ID: a 40-character string like `a4fd5c7e9b3f...`. A branch is **a name written next to one of those IDs**. That is the entire thing. It is a scrap of text on disk. `main` is not your project — `main` is a name pointing at one commit.

You'll rarely see all forty characters. Git prints the first seven — `b9e46c0` — because that is already enough to pick one commit out of thousands. That short form is what appears under the dots in the graph panel, and in the one-line log view you'll meet in a moment. Plain `git log` still prints all forty. Same ID, abbreviated.

body.analogy: Remember the photo album from Module 1. A branch is a **sticky note** stuck to one photo with a name written on it. `main` is a sticky note reading "main". Creating a new branch is writing a second sticky note and putting it on the *same photo*. You have not copied a single photograph. You have spent one sticky note.

body.p: That's why branching is instant, even in a project with a hundred thousand files. Nothing is duplicated. One short line of text gets written, and it takes the same time whether your project is a shopping list or an operating system.

body.h: HEAD: the note that says "you are here"

body.p: There is one more sticky note, and it's a special one. **HEAD** marks which branch you are currently standing on. When `git log` shows you `(HEAD -> main)`, Git is telling you two facts at once: the branch `main` points at this commit, *and* you are currently on `main`.

graph.caption: Two branch names, one commit. Someone ran `git branch neon-theme` a moment ago — the commands are collected at the end of this lesson, so for now watch what happens to the picture rather than the typing. Look closely: both labels sit on the same dot. Nothing was copied, and HEAD says you are still standing on main.

body.h: The branch you're standing on moves

body.p: Here is the part that makes branches useful rather than merely cheap. **When you make a commit, Git slides the sticky note you are standing on forward onto the new commit.** Automatically, every single time. You have been doing this since Module 2 without noticing — it is how `main` kept up with your history.
So if you step onto `neon-theme` and commit there, `neon-theme` moves forward — and `main` stays exactly where it was, because nobody moved it.

graph.caption: One commit later, made while standing on neon-theme. That label moved forward by itself. main did not budge — it is now one commit behind.

body.p: And `main` can move too. Step back onto `main`, make a *different* commit there, and the history genuinely forks: two chains of commits that share a past and disagree about the present.

graph.caption: Diverged. One shared history, two futures. Neither is more real than the other, and nothing has been lost — every commit is still there, each with a name pointing at it.

body.h: What switching does to the files in your folder

body.p: `git switch <name>` does two things. It moves HEAD onto that branch — and it updates the files that *differ* between the commit you were standing on and the commit you're going to.

That word **differ** is doing a lot of work. Git is not repainting your whole folder. Files that are identical on both sides are left completely alone — including any uncommitted edits you happen to have in them. Those come with you.

body.warn: There is a catch in that convenience. An edit that follows you to another branch is still uncommitted when it arrives — and a `git commit` over there will happily record it on the wrong branch. If you are carrying work that belongs somewhere specific, commit it before you switch. Module 9 introduces `git stash`, which exists for exactly this moment.

body.p: This is the moment beginners panic. You switch from `neon-theme` back to `main`, open your stylesheet, and the pink is gone. Worse, a file you created over on the other branch has disappeared from the folder entirely.

body.tip: Nothing was destroyed. Those contents are sitting inside a commit, and the branch name is your bookmark back to them. Switch to that branch and the files reappear exactly as you left them. Your folder is a **window onto one commit at a time**, not the whole album.

body.p: Two details worth knowing before they surprise you:

list: Files Git isn't tracking — the ones `git status` calls **untracked** — are not touched by switching. They sit in the folder wherever you go, like a coffee cup you carry from room to room. The one exception: if the branch you're moving to has a *committed* file with the same name, Git stops and asks you to move or remove yours first. It will not overwrite a file it never recorded.
Anything you have **committed** is reachable through its branch name. Anything you have **not** committed lives only in the folder — which is exactly what the next section is about.

body.p: Git stops you in exactly one situation: when the file you have been editing is one of the files it would have to overwrite. Suppose you're on `main` with an uncommitted edit to `style.css`, and `neon-theme` holds a *different* version of that same file. Switching would mean writing neon's version over the top of yours. Git won't do it:

body.code:
git switch neon-theme
error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by switch:
	style.css
Please commit your changes or stash them before you switch branches.
Aborting

body.tip: Real Git prints that same message but says *overwritten by checkout*, even when you typed `switch`. `switch` and `checkout` share the same machinery underneath and that one word never got updated. Don't let it throw you — it is the same refusal.

body.p: Read it as a favour rather than an obstacle: Git is refusing to throw away work you never recorded. Note how narrow the refusal is — edit a file that both branches agree on and the switch goes ahead, carrying your edit with you. It is only the collision that stops you, and you have two ways out.

list: **Commit the change** on the branch you're currently standing on. It is then safely inside a commit, and the switch costs nothing.
**Stash it** — put the edit on a shelf and take it back down later. `git stash` is Module 9's business. Until then, commit.

body.tip: Creating a branch is different: `git switch -c <name>` never disturbs uncommitted work, because the new branch starts at the very commit you are already standing on — there is nothing for Git to rewrite. So the classic "oh no, I started this on main" moment has a one-command fix: `git switch -c good-idea` takes you *and* your half-finished edit somewhere it belongs.

body.p: When a branch has done its job, `git branch -d <name>` peels the sticky note off. It does not delete the commits — you are throwing away a *label*, not the photographs.

body.warn: `git branch -d` refuses when the branch holds commits that exist nowhere else, saying the branch "is not fully merged". That is a guard rail, not a wall: removing the only name pointing at your work would make it genuinely hard to find again. A capital `-D` overrides the guard. Reach for `-D` only when you have decided, on purpose, to abandon that work.

list: `git branch` — list every branch. The `*` marks where you are standing.
`git branch <name>` — write a new sticky note here, but stay where you are.
`git switch -c <name>` — write a new sticky note here **and** step onto it. The one you'll use most.
`git switch <name>` — step onto an existing branch, updating the files that differ between here and there.
`git branch -d <name>` — retire a branch name you're finished with. You can't delete the one you're standing on.

body.tip: Older tutorials write `git checkout -b <name>` where this course writes `git switch -c <name>`, and `git checkout <name>` where this course writes `git switch <name>`. Same effect. `switch` was added to Git because `checkout` had been given too many unrelated jobs and confused everyone. Both spellings work in this sandbox — prefer `switch`.

body.p: The Cafe Nona site is in front of you, two commits deep and perfectly fine. You want to try a loud neon restyle that you are honestly not sure about, and you'd rather not do it on `main`, where the live site lives.
Keep an eye on the graph panel as you work. This is the module where it earns its keep — you are about to watch a label move on its own, and then watch a history fork in two.

That was instant, and — check the file panel — not one file changed. Here's the proof. `--oneline` squeezes each commit onto a single line (short ID, labels in brackets, message) and `--all` shows every branch's history, not only the one you're standing on. Read the labels in brackets carefully.

body.p: A very ordinary Monday. You're writing a bread book, and you started a new file called `croissants.md` while standing on `main` — everybody does it — before realising, a few lines in, that this experiment deserves a branch of its own. There is also a stray branch called `old-idea` that nobody is ever going back to.

Nothing here needs merging; that's the next module. Nothing needs undoing either. Run `git branch` and `git status` first, look at what you've been handed, and think about **where the commit is going to land** before you make it.

list: A branch is **a name pointing at one commit** — a sticky note, not a copy of your files. That's why creating one is instant however big the project.
**HEAD** is the note that says "you are here". `(HEAD -> main)` means: main points at this commit, and you're standing on main.
When you commit, the branch you're standing on **moves forward with you**. Branches you aren't on stay put — that is precisely how a history forks.

`git switch <name>` updates the files that **differ** between where you were and where you're going. Files change, appear and vanish; files both commits agree on are left alone. Nothing committed is ever lost — the branch name is your way back.

Git refuses to switch only when the move would overwrite an uncommitted edit of yours. Commit it first (or, from Module 9, stash it). `git switch -c` always carries unfinished work along, because the new branch starts where you already are — nothing has to be rewritten.
`git branch` list · `git branch <name>` create · `git switch -c <name>` create and step on · `git switch <name>` step on · `git branch -d <name>` retire

graph.caption: Where this module leaves you: one shared past, two live futures, a sticky note on each. Both are one git switch away.

body.p: Next: those two branches are still strangers to each other. Module 6 introduces them — `git merge`, what a merge commit really is, and what to do when both sides have edited the same line.

modules.title: Merging & Conflicts
modules.summary: How branches come back together: fast-forwards, merge commits, and meeting your first conflict calmly — it is only text, and you can always back out.

body.p: Last module you learned to split your work onto a **branch** — a movable label pointing at a commit, a safe side road for an idea. That is only half the story. Sooner or later the side road has to rejoin the main one, and the work you did over there has to come back. That is **merging**.

`git merge <branch>` always means one thing: *take the branch I name, and bring its work into the branch I am standing on right now*. The branch you name is not changed at all. Only the branch you are standing on moves.

body.tip: Merging is directional, and beginners get it backwards constantly. To get `feature` into `main`, you `git switch main` **first**, then `git merge feature`. Say it out loud before you type: stand where you want the work to land.

body.p: Sometimes there is nothing to reconcile at all. You branched off `main`, did some work, and while you were away nobody touched `main`. Your branch is not a rival version of the project — it is `main` plus a few more commits.

graph.caption: Before the merge. main still sits on the first commit; hours-fix is one commit further along the same road. Nothing on main has moved — that is the fast-forward condition.

body.p: Look at what Git actually has to do here: nothing. Every commit on `hours-fix` already sits in a straight line after `main`'s commit. To bring the work in, Git only has to pick up the `main` label and set it down further along the road it was already on. That is a **fast-forward** — no new commit is made, and the history stays one straight line.

graph.caption: After git merge hours-fix. No new dot appeared. main and hours-fix now label the very same commit.

body.analogy: Remember what Module 5 said happens every time you commit: Git peels the sticky note you are standing on off its photo and re-sticks it to the new one. A fast-forward is that same move, done once, by hand. `hours-fix`'s note is already further down the album; the merge lifts `main`'s note and puts it on the same photo. No photograph is copied, edited, or taken — one sticky note moved.

body.p: Now the interesting case. You branched off, did your work — but `main` moved too while you were away. The two lines of work have **diverged**: neither one is *ahead* of the other in the way `hours-fix` was, because each contains commits the other has never seen. There is no sticky note to slide forward — it would have to leave commits behind.

graph.caption: Diverged. Both sides gained a commit after they parted, so neither branch contains the other.

body.analogy: You and a friend each photocopied the same page of notes and scribbled on your own copy. To combine them you do not lay the two scribbled copies side by side — you put each one next to the *original*. Anything only you touched is plainly yours to keep; anything only they touched is theirs; and the only real argument is a line you both rewrote. The original is the referee.

body.p: Git handles this by looking at **three** commits — which is where the name *three-way merge* comes from. Its referee is the fork point: the last commit both branches shared. It compares that against your side's **tip** and their side's tip — a branch's *tip* is the newest commit it points at, the sticky note's current home. For every part of every file it asks one plain question: *did this change on one side, or on both?*

list: Changed on **only their side** → take their version.
Changed on **only your side** → keep yours.
Changed on **neither** side → nothing to do.

Changed on **both** sides, in the same place, differently → Git stops and asks you. That is a conflict. Note *same place*: if you edited the top of a file while they edited the bottom, real Git combines both without a word.

body.p: When nothing at all lands in that last row, Git can combine both sides by itself, and it records the result as a **merge commit**: the one kind of commit that has **two** parents, one pointing back into each side of the fork.

graph.caption: After the merge. The newest dot is a merge commit — follow the two lines leaving it and you land on both sides of the fork. That fork-and-join shape is what a merge looks like forever after.

body.p: That shape is permanent, and that is a feature. Months later the graph still shows that two lines of work ran side by side and exactly where they came back together. Nothing was flattened or thrown away — every commit from both sides is still in the history, reachable and readable.

Ask yourself one question before you merge: **has the branch I am standing on moved since the other branch split off?** If it has not, you get a fast-forward and no new commit. If it has, you get a merge commit. `git log --oneline --all` shows every branch's tip at once, which is usually enough to see the answer at a glance.

You do not have to predict it, though. Git works it out and tells you: the output says `Fast-forward`, or `Merge made by the 'ort' strategy` — or `Already up to date.`, which means the branch you named holds nothing yours does not already have. That last one is not a failure either; there was nothing to bring over. Knowing which to expect means you are never surprised by your own history.
(`ort` is only the name of the recipe Git used to combine the two sides. You never have to choose it, nothing needs installing, and you can read that line as *merge commit made*.)

body.h: A conflict is not an error

body.p: Here is the sentence to hold on to: **a merge conflict is not a failure, not a bug, and not damage to your project.** It is Git being careful. Two people wrote different words in the same place; Git has no opinion about English, so it refuses to guess and hands the decision to the only one qualified to make it.

body.analogy: Two people are editing the same shopping list. One crosses out 'milk' and writes 'oat milk'; the other writes 'whole milk'. A robot combining those lists cannot possibly know which you meant. A careful robot does not flip a coin — it writes both suggestions onto the line, hands you the pen, and waits.

body.p: When Git stops, it says so in plain words. Here the `bold-tagline` branch had changed two files — the tagline and the opening hours — and only one of them clashed:

body.code:
$ git merge bold-tagline
Auto-merging tagline.txt
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in tagline.txt
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

body.p: This terminal prints that CONFLICT line in red. Real Git prints it plainly — but it does finish with a *something needs your attention* status, and the `git status` you are about to run colours the stuck file red on your own machine too. Either way it is a flag, not a verdict on your work.

Notice that Git names the stuck file twice. `Auto-merging tagline.txt` is Git saying it *tried* to combine that file; the CONFLICT line underneath says it could not. Everything it could merge, it already merged — if ten files changed and one clashed, the other nine are done and sitting in your staging area. The merge is now **paused**: half finished, holding still until you say what to do.
`git status` is at its most helpful in this state. It names what is stuck, and hands you both exits:

body.code:
$ git status
On branch main
You have unmerged paths.
  (fix conflicts and run "git commit")
  (use "git merge --abort" to abort the merge)

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
	modified:   hours.txt

Unmerged paths:
  (use "git add <file>..." to mark resolution)
	both modified:   tagline.txt

body.p: Two lists. The top one is work Git already finished for you — `hours.txt` came across cleanly and is staged, ready to go. Only the bottom one is waiting on a human.

body.h: The conflict markers, line by line

body.p: Open the conflicted file and you will find something like this. Beginners find it alarming — it looks like the file has been vandalised. It has not. Those are ordinary lines of text that Git typed into your file, and you can delete them with the same keyboard you delete anything else.

body.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD
Good coffee, no fuss.
=======
Wake up and taste the sunrise.
>>>>>>> bold-tagline

list: `<<<<<<< HEAD` opens the block. Everything below it, down to the `=======`, is **your** version — what the branch you are standing on says. `HEAD` is Git's word for *where you are right now*.
`=======` is the fence in the middle. Above it, yours. Below it, theirs. It belongs to neither side and is not part of anybody's text.
`>>>>>>> bold-tagline` closes the block. Everything above it, back up to the `=======`, is **their** version — and the name after the arrows tells you which branch it came from.

body.p: That is the entire format. Nothing is hidden, nothing is encoded, and there is no way to break it by reading it. On your own machine, a file with three separate clashes in it shows three of these blocks, one after another. (This sandbox compares whole files, so here you will only ever meet one block per file.)

body.h: Resolving: three moves, always in this order

body.p: Settling a conflict is the same small loop every single time, once per conflicted file:

list: **1. Edit the file** so it says what you actually want, and delete all three marker lines. Keep your side, keep their side, keep both, or write a third thing that is neither — Git does not check and has no preference.
**2. `git add <file>`** — during a merge, `add` carries an extra meaning: *I have settled this one*. It is how you tell Git the file is no longer in dispute.
**3. `git commit`** — this concludes the merge and creates the merge commit. You can leave off `-m` here: mid-merge, Git offers a sensible default message such as `Merge branch 'bold-tagline'`.

body.tip: On your own machine that last step does not finish silently. Git opens a text editor showing the default message already written for you, and the merge is not committed until you save and close it (in vim: press `Esc`, type `:wq`, press Enter — in nano: `Ctrl-O`, Enter, `Ctrl-X`). Nothing has gone wrong when that happens. If you would rather skip the editor entirely, `git commit --no-edit` accepts the default message straight away — and that works in this sandbox too. Plain `git commit` works here as well, because there is no editor to open.

body.p: This sandbox has no text editor, so step 1 is done by overwriting the whole file: `echo "the line you want" > tagline.txt`. That is a tidy way to do it anyway — writing the file fresh removes the marker lines automatically.

body.warn: Deleting every marker is your job, and it is easy to leave one behind — a stray `=======` halfway down a long file. Git will commit it without complaint, because to Git it is only text. Read the file once more before you `git add` it.

body.p: Suppose you start the merge, look at the mess, and decide today is not the day. Type `git merge --abort`. Every file snaps back to exactly how it was before you typed `git merge`, the markers vanish, and Git forgets the merge ever started. It prints nothing at all, which is its way of saying *fine, done*.

Nothing is lost. Both branches still sit exactly where they were, with all their commits. You can come back and try the merge again in five minutes, or next week, with someone else sitting beside you.

body.tip: `git merge --abort` is the reason you never need to be afraid of *starting* a merge. Attempt it; if you do not like what you find, back out. Until you make that final commit, the whole thing is reversible.

body.warn: One way this sandbox is blunter than real Git: it compares whole files, so it reports a conflict whenever the same file changed on both sides. Real Git compares line by line and will merge edits to different parts of one file without a murmur. Everything else here — the markers, the three-move loop, `--abort` — behaves as it does on your own machine, with one cosmetic exception: real Git opens a text editor for the merge message where this sandbox writes it for you.

body.p: You are back on the Luna Cafe site, and two branches are waiting for you. `hours-fix` corrects the opening hours and was started from exactly where `main` stands today. `bold-tagline` was started earlier in the week — before you sat down and rewrote the tagline yourself.

steps.say: Get the lay of the land before touching anything. `--all` tells the log to show every branch's commits, not only the branch you are on. Read it bottom-up: everything grew out of **Publish the cafe site**, and each name in brackets marks where that branch label currently sits.

Merge the easy one first. `hours-fix` was started from `main`'s current commit, so `main` has nothing of its own to protect. Watch for the word **Fast-forward** in the output — and notice the graph gains no new dot. The `main` label slid one commit to the right.
steps.hint: Type: git merge hours-fix — you are already standing on main, which is where the work should land.

expect.label: main has 3 commits — no merge commit was created
Nothing left over in the working tree

steps.say: Now the other one. `bold-tagline` was created *before* you wrote your own tagline, so both sides have changed `tagline.txt` since they parted — and they disagree about what it should say. Run the merge and read every line of the output. Nothing here is broken.
steps.hint: Type: git merge bold-tagline — expect it to stop with the word CONFLICT. That is the whole point of this lesson.

expect.label: The merge paused with a conflict in tagline.txt

steps.say: First ask the compass. Git names the file that is stuck under **Unmerged paths**, and spells out both exits: fix it and commit, or abort. Then look at what it actually wrote into the file — your version sits under `<<<<<<< HEAD`, theirs sits under the `=======` fence, and `>>>>>>> bold-tagline` closes the block and names where it came from. Three lines of ordinary text. That is the entire horror show. Just the one list this time: `bold-tagline` changed only `tagline.txt`, so there was nothing for Git to finish cleanly alongside it. When a branch touches several files and only one of them clashes, a second list appears above this one — the work Git already did for you.
steps.hint: Type: git status — then: cat tagline.txt

steps.say: Before fixing anything, prove to yourself that you can walk away. `git merge --abort` rewinds to the moment before you typed `git merge`: markers gone, both branches untouched, merge forgotten. It prints nothing — that is Git saying *fine, done*. Do not settle the file yet — you are going to walk back into this same conflict in a moment and finish it properly.
steps.hint: Type: git merge --abort. (If you already finished the merge instead, press ↺ reset to restore the starting state and pick it up again from step 2.)

steps.say: Good — that escape hatch is always there. Now walk back in on purpose. Same command, same conflict, except this time you are going to settle it.

expect.label: You are back in the conflict, deliberately

steps.say: Resolve it by writing the line you actually want. Here we borrow from both taglines. On your own machine you could keep either side untouched or invent something else entirely — Git has no opinion. This checklist only asks for a line of your own that still mentions coffee. Writing the whole file in one go also wipes the three marker lines, which is exactly what you need.
steps.cmd: echo "Wake up to good coffee. No fuss." > tagline.txt
steps.hint: Type: echo "Wake up to good coffee. No fuss." > tagline.txt — or any line of your own that mentions coffee.

expect.label: tagline.txt now says something about coffee

steps.say: Editing the file is **not** enough — as far as Git is concerned the dispute is still open. `git add` is how you say *this one is settled*. It is the same command you have used since module 2, quietly doing a second job in the middle of a merge.

Conclude the merge. Notice there is no `-m` this time: mid-merge, Git has a sensible default message ready. This sandbox accepts it for you; on your own machine an editor would open with that message in it, and `git commit --no-edit` skips the editor. Then look at the graph — the new dot reaches back into both sides of the fork. It has finally closed.
steps.hint: Type: git commit — no -m needed while a merge is in progress. (git commit --no-edit works too.)

expect.label: main's newest commit is a merge commit with two parents

body.p: Three friends are planning a trip in one shared repository. You raised the budget on `main` after the flights went up. Sam, off on a branch, raised it too — to a different number — and also added a rain jacket to the packing list. Meanwhile somebody added a day trip to Porto on a third branch.

Two branches are waiting, and one of them is going to fight you. Take any route you like — the checklist watches the end state, not the commands you type. And remember `git merge --abort` exists, so you genuinely cannot get stuck.

Finish with a clean working tree and no merge still in progress.

When the conflict appears, run git status. It shows two separate lists: the files Git already merged for you, and the one file it wants you to settle. Only that one file needs your attention.
Overwrite the conflicted file with the single line you want and nothing else: echo "Budget: 500 each" > budget.txt — writing it fresh wipes the three marker lines at the same time.
Editing is not enough. git add budget.txt marks it resolved, then git commit concludes the merge (no -m needed). Then merge the other branch the same way.

Sam's branch is merged into main
No conflict markers left in budget.txt
Sam's rain jacket survived the merge
Every commit from both branches is still in main's history

list: `git merge <branch>` brings the named branch's work **into the branch you are standing on**. Switch to the destination first.
**Fast-forward**: your branch never moved, so Git slides its label forward. No new commit, history stays a straight line.
**Three-way merge**: both sides moved, so Git compares the fork point against both tips and records a **merge commit** with two parents.
A **conflict** happens only where both sides changed the same thing differently. Git merges everything else for you first, and says so.
A conflict is not an error. It is Git declining to guess — and it is completely reversible right up until you commit.
`Already up to date.` is a third possible answer: the branch you named holds nothing yours does not already have, so there was nothing to bring over.

body.code:
git merge <branch>       # CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in <file>
git status               # which file is stuck, and both ways out

# 1. edit <file>: keep what you want, delete <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>>
git add <file>           # "this one is settled"
git commit               # concludes the merge (or --no-edit, to skip the editor)

git merge --abort        # or: back out entirely, any time before that commit

body.p: Everything so far has happened on one computer. Next: **remotes** — putting your repository somewhere other people can reach, and pulling their work back down.

modules.title: Remotes & Push/Pull
modules.summary: A remote is a whole other copy of your repository living somewhere else. How to send work to it, how to get work from it, and why origin/main is a memory rather than a branch.

lessons.title: Your repo's twin in the cloud

body.p: Everything you have built so far lives in exactly one place: this folder, on this computer. That has been fine for learning. It is not fine for real work, for two reasons. One spilled coffee and the project is gone. And nobody else can help you — there is nothing for them to help *on*.
Both problems have the same fix, and it is the last big idea in everyday Git.

body.h: A remote is a whole other repository

body.p: A **remote** is another complete copy of your repository that lives somewhere else — usually on a server you can reach over the internet (GitHub, GitLab, your company's machine), sometimes on a colleague's laptop.

Read that again, because beginners nearly always read it wrong. A remote is not a backup of your files. It is not a folder in the cloud. It is a **repository**: every commit, every message, the whole album, sitting in a second place.

body.analogy: You and a friend each keep a photo album of the same trip. The album on the shelf in their house is the remote. It is a real album, not a photocopy of yours — and neither album updates itself. If you want their new photos, you ask for them. If you want them to have yours, you post them.

body.warn: Git is not Dropbox. Saving a file doesn't sync. Committing doesn't sync either. Nothing you do reaches the remote until you run `git push`, and nothing of theirs reaches you until you run `git fetch` or `git pull`. That is not a missing feature — it is the whole design. You decide what crosses, and when.

body.h: Introducing your repo to a remote

body.p: In the real world you usually meet a remote from the other direction: `git clone <url>` copies an entire repository down onto your machine and wires up the connection for you in one step. That is how you will join most projects. This sandbox has no network, so `git clone` here will politely tell you so — we will wire the connection up by hand instead, which lands in exactly the same place.

`git remote add origin <url>` tells your repository: *there is another copy of us over there, and I am going to call it `origin`*. The word `origin` is a nickname and nothing more — it is the conventional name for "the remote this project came from". You could call it `sam` or `server`; everyone calls it `origin`, so we will too.
`git remote -v` prints the nicknames you have saved and the URLs hiding behind them. The `v` is for *verbose*.

body.code:
git remote add origin https://github.com/you/iceland-trip.git

git remote -v
# origin   https://github.com/you/iceland-trip.git (fetch)
# origin   https://github.com/you/iceland-trip.git (push)

body.p: Here is the whole ceremony of putting a project of your own on the internet, start to finish. You make a new empty repository on GitHub (or GitLab, or wherever); the site shows you a URL. Then, in your project folder on your machine:

body.code:
git init                       # only if it isn't a repository yet
git add .
git commit -m "First commit"
git remote add origin https://github.com/you/iceland-trip.git
git push -u origin main

body.p: Five lines and your project is on the internet. The URL comes from the site; everything else you already know except the last line, which is next.

body.h: push: send my commits over there

body.p: `git push` uploads the commits on your current branch to the remote. The very first time, you type a slightly longer version:

body.code:
git push -u origin main
# Enumerating objects: 5, done.
# To https://github.com/you/iceland-trip.git
#  * [new branch]      main -> main
# branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.

body.p: The `-u` (long form: `--set-upstream`) is a one-time piece of bookkeeping. It records the pairing "my `main` goes with `origin`'s `main`" — Git calls that the **upstream**. From then on you can type a bare `git push`, or a bare `git pull`, and Git already knows which remote and which branch you mean.

body.tip: Forget the `-u` on your first push and nothing bad happens: Git stops and prints the exact command to type instead. It is a nudge, not a disaster. This is the whole of it:

body.code:
git push
# fatal: The current branch main has no upstream branch.
# To push the current branch and set the remote as upstream, use
#
#     git push --set-upstream origin main

body.warn: `git push` sends **commits**. Edits you have not committed do not go anywhere — there is no such thing as pushing an unsaved file. If you want it on the remote, commit it first.

body.h: The idea this whole module rests on: origin/main

body.p: You are about to meet three things with maddeningly similar names. Go slowly here — very nearly every confusion people have about remotes comes from blurring these together.

list: `main` — your branch, in your repository, on your computer. You move it by committing.
`origin/main` — a label that lives **inside your repository** and records where `origin`'s `main` was **the last time you talked to the remote**. It is local, and you never move it by hand.
`origin`'s actual `main` — the branch as it exists on the server right now. You cannot see it without asking over the network.

body.p: So `origin/main` is not the remote's branch. It is your **memory** of the remote's branch. Once that clicks, `fetch` and `pull` stop being interchangeable magic words and become two plainly different jobs.

body.analogy: `origin/main` is the last photo you have of a friend. It isn't your friend — it is a record of how they looked when you last met. They may have had a haircut this morning; your photo will keep showing the old hair until you see them again. `git fetch` is seeing them again.

body.tip: This course draws you a graph panel. The real world does not — so here is how you answer "where do I stand relative to origin?" without one. Real `git status` says it in words: *"Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 1 commit"*, or *"Your branch and 'origin/main' have diverged"*. And `git log --oneline` prints the same `main` and `origin/main` labels you are watching in the panel, next to the commits they point at — that one works in real Git and in this sandbox alike. (This sandbox's `git status` is the quieter of the two and leaves the ahead/behind line out, so lean on `git log --oneline` while you are here.)

body.p: Here is your repository the moment after a successful push. Your memory of the remote is accurate, because you were just there:

graph.caption: Straight after git push: main and origin/main sit on the same commit. Your record of the remote matches reality.

body.p: Now your teammate Sam commits something and pushes it. Your computer gets no notification. No file of yours changes. No label of yours moves. As far as your repository is concerned, absolutely nothing has happened:

graph.caption: The remote now has a third commit — the bare dot on the right, with no label of yours pointing at it. origin/main still sits one commit back, because nobody has told your repo anything.

body.p: This course's diagram can draw Sam's commit, because it can see the whole simulation. Your repository cannot. Watch the **labels**, not the dots — the labels are what your repo actually knows.

body.h: fetch updates your memory; pull updates your memory and your work

body.p: `git fetch` contacts the remote, downloads any commits you are missing, and moves your `origin/...` labels to match what it found. That is the entire job. It does not touch your branch, your files, or your staging area.

body.tip: `git fetch` cannot damage anything you are working on. It is the safest command in Git. So if you are ever curious what the others have been up to, fetch — nothing will move under your feet.

body.p: `git pull` is two commands wearing one coat:

body.code: git pull   ==   git fetch   +   git merge origin/main

body.p: The fetch half is safe. The merge half is a real merge — the same one from Module 6 — so it rewrites files in your working directory, and if you and Sam edited the same lines you will get the same conflict markers you already know how to resolve.

Most pulls are gentler than that. If you have made no commits of your own since you last synced, the merge half has nothing to reconcile: your branch slides forward onto their commits and Git prints `Fast-forward`, with no merge commit at all. That is the ordinary, everyday pull. You get a merge commit only when both sides committed since you last agreed — the fork drawn further down.

body.warn: Modern Git (2.34 and later) wants you to say once how you like your diverged branches reconciled before it will do it. The first time you pull with commits on both sides it stops on `fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches`. Nothing is broken and nothing is lost — you answer it once with `git config pull.rebase false` in this project, or `git config --global pull.rebase false` for every project on the machine. That asks for merging, which is the behaviour taught here, and the message never comes back. This sandbox has no `git config` and no preference to set, so `git pull` merges straight away.

body.tip: Nervous is good, and you are allowed to look before you leap. Fetch, then read: `git show origin/main` prints the newest incoming commit, message and diff, and that really is what is about to arrive. You can also run `git diff main origin/main` — but read that one carefully. It compares two snapshots in both directions, so Sam's new work shows as `+` lines while your own commits, which the remote has never seen, show as `-` lines. Nothing is about to be deleted. You are looking at the difference between two photographs, not at a plan of action.

body.warn: `git pull` will not run over uncommitted edits. Real Git stops when the incoming merge would touch a file you have edited, and names those files: *"Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by merge."* This sandbox is stricter — it stops while **any tracked file** has uncommitted changes, so it may name a file the merge would never have touched. (Brand-new untracked files are fine; Git is not watching them yet.) Either way it is protecting unsaved work rather than being broken, and either way the cure is the same: commit your changes (or stash them — Module 9) and pull again.

body.h: ! [rejected] — the message everybody meets on day one

body.p: Picture the situation that causes it. You and Sam both started this morning from "Add a packing list". You committed. Sam committed and pushed first. The two histories have now forked:

graph.caption: One fork, three names. Your main is on 'Pack for the rain'. The unlabelled dot is Sam's commit, which the server has. And origin/main — your memory of the server — is still back on 'Add a packing list', where you last looked.

body.p: Look hard at where your memory is sitting. Your repository still believes the remote is on "Add a packing list" — so from where your repository stands, your push is a simple step forward onto the end of the branch, nothing unusual about it. The server knows otherwise.
You run `git push`, and Git says no:

body.code:
To https://github.com/you/iceland-trip.git
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'https://github.com/you/iceland-trip.git'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not
hint: have locally. This is usually caused by another repository pushing to
hint: the same ref. If you want to integrate the remote changes, use
hint: 'git pull' before pushing again.

body.p: Read it as it is meant: *the remote has work you do not have; if I let your push through, Sam's commit would be knocked off the end of the branch and nobody would have it.* Git is refusing to lose somebody's work. It is on your side.

Git words this rejection two ways depending on what you already know. If you have not fetched, you get `(fetch first)`, as above. If you have already fetched — so Sam's commit is sitting in your repository, merely not on your branch — you get `! [rejected]  main -> main (non-fast-forward)` instead, and the hint changes to *"the tip of your current branch is behind its remote counterpart"*. The two mean the same thing: the remote has commits your branch does not contain. (This sandbox always prints the `(fetch first)` wording.)

And notice that either way the fix starts with catching your memory up. That is why the hint says *fetch first*: your record of the remote has to become true before anything you do next can be based on the truth.
The cure is in the hint, and it is always the same three beats:

list: **Pull** — bring their commits down and merge them with yours, in your repository, where a mistake is cheap.
**Fix** — resolve any conflict the merge raises, and check the result still makes sense.
**Push** — your history now contains theirs, so the remote can accept it without losing anything.

body.warn: There is a `git push --force`, which orders the remote to throw its version away and take yours. It has legitimate uses that you do not have yet. It is also exactly how people delete a colleague's afternoon. Never reach for it to make an error message go away.

body.p: You and Sam are planning a trip in a shared repository. Yours is already connected to `origin` — you pushed it last week. This morning you thought of something for the packing list. So, it turns out, did Sam.
Watch the graph panel as you go, and in particular watch **when the `origin/main` label moves** — and when it stubbornly does not.

steps.say: First, who is this repository connected to? `git remote -v` lists every remote nickname and the URL behind it. One remote, nicknamed `origin`, fetch and push — those two lines are the whole connection. Somebody once ran `git remote add origin https://github.com/you/iceland-trip.git` and then `git push -u origin main`; this is what that left behind.
Now look at your history. Two commits — and notice the labels on the newest one: **HEAD -> main, origin/main**. Your branch and your memory of the remote's branch are in the same place.

Do your morning's work: add a line to the packing list and commit it. (`>>` appends a line to the end of a file — the single `>` you met in Module 1 would replace everything in it. And `git commit -am` stages every *tracked* file that changed and commits in one move. Tracked only: a brand-new file Git has never seen still needs its own `git add`.) Notice in the graph that `main` steps forward and `origin/main` does not — committing sends nothing anywhere.
steps.cmd:
echo "- waterproof trousers" >> packing.md
git commit -am "Pack for the rain"
steps.hint: Two commands: echo "- waterproof trousers" >> packing.md — then git commit -am "Pack for the rain"

steps.say: Before pushing, ask the remote whether anything changed while you were typing. `git fetch` downloads what is new and moves your `origin/main` label — and does nothing else at all; your files are untouched. Read the last line of the output: `origin/main` just jumped forward. Sam has been busy.

You now *have* Sam's commit, but it is not part of your branch yet — so you can read it before letting it anywhere near your files. `git show origin/main` prints the newest commit on your memory of the remote: its message and its diff. (The sandbox signs every commit with your own name, so ignore the Author line and picture Sam's there.)

A budget file — harmless, and it touches none of your files. Bring it into your branch with `git pull` (fetch, then merge `origin/main` into `main`). You already fetched a moment ago, so there is nothing new to download and you will only see the merge half do any work. You and Sam both built on the same commit, so this is a three-way merge: Git makes a merge commit joining the two lines of work, exactly like Module 6.

expect.label: Sam's work is part of your main now
A merge commit joins the two histories
budget.md has arrived in your folder

steps.say: Look at the history now. Your commit, Sam's commit, and a merge commit on top — with `origin/main` still sitting back on Sam's commit. Pulling brought their work to you; it sent nothing of yours to them.

expect.label: You saw the merge in the history

steps.say: Finish the round trip. Your history now contains Sam's commit, so the remote can accept yours without losing anything — this push goes through. Notice what you did *not* have to type: no remote, no branch name. That is the `-u` from this repo's very first push paying out; the pairing was recorded once, so a bare `git push` is now unambiguous. Check the labels afterwards: `main` and `origin/main` are together again, and the two copies of the repository match.

body.p: A week later, same trip, same repository. You have been writing all morning and committed none of it. While you were writing, Sam pushed **twice**.

Get everything onto the remote without losing a word of anybody's work. Expect Git to refuse you at least once along the way — when it does, read the message all the way to the bottom. It tells you what to do next.
