exercise.goal: Get your uncommitted work — the new swimsuit line in `packing.md`, and the brand-new file `gear.md` — all the way onto the remote, while keeping both of Sam's commits. Finish with: `origin`'s `main` and your `main` on the same commit; that commit holding Sam's `budget.md` (including his `food 150` line) as well as both of your changes; and a completely clean working tree — nothing modified, nothing untracked.
hints: Start with `git status`, then `git fetch`. Fetching is free and it shows you what the remote has been up to without touching a single file of yours.

In this sandbox `git pull` stops while any tracked file has uncommitted changes, so commit your work first: `git add .` then `git commit -m "..."`. (Remember `gear.md` is brand new — `git commit -am` would walk right past it.)
Now try `git push`, and read the rejection carefully. The hint at the bottom of it names the command that fixes this.
The full loop: commit your work, `git pull` to merge Sam's commits into yours, then `git push` to send the combined history back.

expect.label: origin's main and your main are on the same commit
Your packing list line is committed
Sam's two commits are part of your history now
Sam's budget.md, food line and all, is in your latest commit

list: A **remote** is a whole other copy of the repository, somewhere else. `origin` is the nickname you gave its URL, nothing more.
Nothing crosses between the two copies unless you ask. `git push` sends; `git fetch` and `git pull` receive.
`origin/main` is **not** the remote's branch — it is your record of where the remote's branch was the last time you talked to it.

`git fetch` updates that record and nothing else, so it can never disturb your work. `git pull` = `git fetch` + `git merge origin/main`, and the merge half *does* change your files. If you have committed nothing yourself, that merge is a `Fast-forward` and no merge commit appears; you get a merge commit only when both sides have moved.
`! [rejected] ... (fetch first)` means the remote has commits you do not. Pull, fix anything the merge raises, push. Never `--force` your way past it.

Push sends commits, not edits — uncommitted work stays on your machine. And `git commit -am` only sweeps up files Git already tracks, so a brand-new file still needs its own `git add` before it can travel anywhere.

body.code:
git remote add origin <url>   attach a remote and nickname it origin
git remote -v                 list your remotes and their URLs
git push -u origin main       first push; records main <-> origin/main
git push                      send this branch's new commits
git fetch                     move the origin/* labels; touch nothing else
git pull                      fetch, then merge origin/main into your branch

graph.caption: The state worth ending every working session in: main and origin/main on the same commit, everything committed and sent.

body.p: Next: remotes and branches together. Module 8 walks the loop real teams live in — branch off, push the branch, get it reviewed, merge it back — the feature-branch workflow, end to end.

modules.title: Collaboration Basics
modules.summary: The loop real teams run every day: sync main, branch, commit, push, open a pull request, merge, delete. What a pull request actually is, and how to be someone people like reviewing.

body.p: You already know every command in this module. `switch -c`, `commit`, `push`, `pull`, `merge`, `branch -d` — that's the whole toolkit, and you've used all of it. What you haven't seen is the **order** teams run them in, and the reasoning that produced the order. That order has a name — the *feature-branch workflow* — and some version of it runs at nearly every place that writes software.

list: **Sync** — bring your local `main` up to date with everyone else's.
**Branch** — cut a new branch for this one piece of work.
**Work** — edit, stage, commit. As many commits as the work honestly needs.
**Push** — send the branch to the shared copy.
**Open a pull request** — in a browser, ask for your branch to be merged.
**Review** — someone reads it and asks questions; you push fixes to the same branch.
**Merge** — your commits join `main`.
**Sync back** — `git switch main`, `git pull`. The merge happened on the server; this brings it down to you.
**Delete the branch** — it did its job.

body.p: Round and round, several times a week, for years. Eight of those nine steps are commands you can already type. The interesting question isn't *how* — it's *why this shape*.

body.h: So what is a pull request?

body.p: The honest part first: there is no `git pull-request` command, and there never will be. Git has no idea pull requests exist. A pull request is a feature of the **website** your team's repository lives on — GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket — and it is exactly what its name says: a request that someone pull your branch into theirs.

Concretely it is one page with two halves. One half is a **diff**: every change your branch has made *since it left* `main`, laid out file by file — measured from the point the two lines diverged, not against wherever `main` has got to since. The other half is a **conversation**: comments on individual lines, questions, suggested edits, and eventually an approval. When somebody clicks **Merge**, the website runs a merge on a server — the closest thing you can run yourself is a `git merge` on `main`.

body.analogy: A pull request is the note you clip to a manuscript before handing it to your editor. The manuscript — your branch — is finished as far as you're concerned. The note says: here's what I changed and why; please read it, and if you're happy, fold it into the edition that goes to the printers. The margin notes and your replies are the review. Nothing reaches the printed book until someone says yes.

graph.caption: What a pull request is looking at. `main` and `origin/main` sit on the same commit — your machine and the shared copy agree about the trunk — while `add-faq` runs one commit ahead of both. That gap, the commit your branch has that `main` doesn't, is the diff a reviewer is handed.

body.tip: Real git spells that comparison with three dots: `git diff main...your-branch`, meaning "everything my branch did since the two diverged". This sandbox doesn't accept the three-dot form, so keep it as vocabulary for later — while `main` hasn't moved, the two-ref `git diff main your-branch` you already know shows the same thing.

GitLab calls the identical thing a **merge request**, which is frankly the better name — "pull" describes what the maintainer does at the far end, not what you're asking for. Same object, different word. Don't let the vocabulary throw you.

body.warn: This sandbox has no network and no browser, so it cannot open a real pull request. Everything git does in the loop — branch, commit, push, merge, delete — you will run for real. When we reach the browser half, I'll say so plainly, and then you'll play the website yourself: merge locally and push the result, which is the closest thing you can run locally to what the Merge button does on your behalf. Not identical: the real button usually records a merge commit even when a fast-forward would do, and some teams pick *Squash* instead, which folds your whole branch into one brand-new commit. Same idea, different shape of history.

body.h: Why the loop is shaped like this

body.p: Every step exists to protect one promise: **`main` always works.** Anyone should be able to take `main` at any moment — to deploy it (put it in front of real users), demo it, or branch from it — and find it in one piece. Your branch is the opposite: it's where things are *allowed* to be broken, half-finished and ugly, because nobody else is standing on it. The pull request is the door between the two, and review is the lock.

body.h: Branch from the newest main you can get

body.p: That's what the `git pull` at the top of the loop is for. A branch cut from a stale `main` shows your reviewer a diff against code that has already moved on, and everything `main` gained in the meantime turns into a merge you'll have to do later, in a hurry, under someone else's deadline.

body.tip: Work you haven't committed yet isn't attached to any branch — it sits in your working directory and comes with you when you switch. So a file you started on `main` by mistake is easy to rehome: cut the branch, then commit it there. Nothing was ever on `main` except in your head.

body.h: Short branches merge; long branches negotiate

body.p: A branch is a bet that the rest of the world will hold still while you work. It won't. Every day your branch lives, `main` drifts further from the ground you built on. A branch that lives a day merges quietly. A branch that lives three weeks becomes a negotiation — with the code, and usually with a person.

graph.caption: One afternoon, two people. Your branch left main at 'Add a readme'; while it was away, Priya's opening-hours commit landed on main. Note that pulling first did not stop main moving after you branched — nothing can; that is exactly why short branches are easier. The last dot is the merge that folds the two lines back together, and the longer your branch lives, the more there is to fold.

body.p: So the size of your branch is a choice you make at the start, not a fact you discover at the end. If a piece of work is too big to finish in a day or two, that's information: find the first useful slice of it, ship that, and branch again.

body.tip: Before you ask anyone to look, sync your branch: `git switch main` → `git pull` → `git switch your-branch` → `git merge main`. Now the branch shows the *result* of your change against today's code rather than last Tuesday's, and any conflicts are yours to solve calmly, instead of ambushing whoever clicks Merge.

body.h: How to be reviewed, and how to review

body.p: Reviews catch bugs. That's the advertised benefit and the smallest one. The real payoff is that a second person now understands this part of the project, and that writing "here's what I did and why" makes you notice things you'd otherwise have shipped.

One mechanical thing that trips up everyone the first time: a pull request is not a frozen submission. It **watches the branch**. When a reviewer asks for a change, you fix it on the same branch, commit, and `git push` — and the pull request page updates itself, diff and all. No second pull request, no re-uploading anything. That is the whole reason review comments are cheap to act on.

list: **Keep the diff small.** A forty-line change gets careful, specific comments. A two-thousand-line change gets "looks good to me". Reviewer attention is a budget — decide what you're spending it on.
**Write the description for someone who wasn't in your head.** What changed, why it changed, and how to check that it works.

**Review the code, not the person.** "This loop runs twice" — not "you always do this". When you're unsure, ask a question instead of delivering a verdict; you'll be wrong often enough to be glad you did.
**Reply to every comment**, even if the reply is "good catch, fixed". Silence reads as a shrug.
**An approval is a signature.** If you don't understand a change, say so and ask. That's a legitimate review outcome, not a failure of nerve.

body.warn: The one habit worth being strict about: on a shared project, don't commit straight to `main` — not even for a one-line typo fix. Git will happily let you. But it's the single path with no second pair of eyes, and "tiny" fixes are exactly the ones that turn out to touch something you'd forgotten about.

list: **Git, on your machine:** `switch -c`, `add`, `commit`, `push`, `fetch` / `pull`, `merge`, `branch -d`.
**The website:** the pull request page, the side-by-side diff, comments and approvals, automated test runs, the Merge button, and the button that deletes the branch afterwards.

body.p: None of the website's half is magic — every button is running git commands on a server somewhere. Which is why, when the buttons confuse you, the questions that get you unstuck are the ones you already own: which branch is this? What commits does it have that `main` doesn't? What would merging it actually do?

You're on a two-person project: a little site for a hiking club, already connected to `origin`. Your teammate Priya has been working while you were away. Your job today is one small page — and one full trip around the loop, from syncing `main` to deleting the branch behind you.
Every command below you have run before. The thing to learn here is the *sequence*, and what each step buys you. Watch the graph redraw as you go.

body.p: The mental model: **`main` is a promise that always holds; a branch is a place where it doesn't have to.** A pull request is the door between them, and every step of the loop exists to keep that door working.

list: `git switch main` + `git pull` — start from what everyone else already has.
`git switch -c add-faq` — one branch per piece of work, named after the work.
`git add` + `git commit -m "…"` — as many commits as the work needs.
`git push -u origin add-faq` — now it exists off your laptop and the team can see it. The `-u` is for the first push only.
**Open the pull request in the browser** — git has no command for this, and never will.

`git merge add-faq` on `main`, then `git push` — here that's us standing in for the Merge button; on a real project the server merges when someone clicks it, and you run `git switch main` + `git pull` instead to bring the merge down to you.
`git branch -d add-faq` — the branch is spent; the commits stay in `main`.

body.p: Next: undoing mistakes. Reset, revert, stash and the reflog — the module where you find out how little of what beginners fear is actually unrecoverable.

modules.title: Undoing Mistakes
modules.summary: Pick the right undo by asking two questions: has it been committed, and has it been shared? amend, reset, revert, stash — and the reflog that makes almost everything recoverable.

body.p: Sooner or later you will type a Git command, read the output, and feel your stomach drop. The commit you meant to fix has vanished. The file you spent an hour on is suddenly three lines long. Everyone who uses Git has had that moment.

So let's start with the reassuring part: **Git is remarkably reluctant to lose your work.** Once something has been committed it is written into the repository and it stays there — even after you think you've deleted it. Nearly every disaster in this module is a few keystrokes away from being fixed. By the end of this lesson you'll know which keystrokes.

There are about six commands people reach for when undoing things, and beginners try to memorise all six at once. You don't have to. You only ever need to answer two questions about the thing you regret:

list: **Has it been committed yet?** If the change is still sitting in your working directory or staging area, no history is involved at all and undoing it is cheap.

**Has it been shared?** Once you have pushed a commit — or a teammate has pulled it — other people's copies of the history contain it. Rewriting it now means their story of the past and yours no longer agree.

body.analogy: Picture your work moving through three stages. A change you haven't committed is **a note on your desk**: crumple it, nobody ever saw it. A commit you haven't pushed is **a page in your private notebook**: you can tear it out and rewrite it, and no one will ever know. A commit you have pushed is **a story printed in the newspaper**: you cannot un-print it. What you do instead is print a correction in tomorrow's edition.

body.p: Desk, notebook, newspaper. Those are the three flavors of undo, and each one has its own tools.
You edited a file, or staged something, and you want to walk it back. You met the first of these in Module 3:

body.code:
git restore --staged notes.txt   # take it back out of the staging area, keep the edit
git restore notes.txt            # throw the edit away, back to the staged version
                                 # (or the committed one, if nothing is staged)

body.warn: `git restore --staged` is completely safe — your edits stay in the file, they're just no longer in frame for the next photo. `git restore` **without** `--staged` is a different animal: it overwrites your file with whatever is in the staging area — which, if you haven't staged anything, is the last committed version. That's why undoing a mistake you had already staged takes both commands: `git restore --staged <file>` first, then `git restore <file>`. And those thrown-away edits were never recorded anywhere, so nothing can bring them back — not even the reflog you'll meet at the end of this lesson. It is the one command here with no safety net.

body.p: There's a gentler option when you don't want to lose the work at all — you just want it *out of the way*. Perhaps you're halfway through a change and something urgent needs the file clean first.

body.analogy: `git stash` is the drawer you sweep your desk into when a visitor knocks. The desk is instantly tidy; the work isn't gone, it's in the drawer. `git stash pop` tips the drawer back out onto the desk.

body.code:
git stash        # shelve every uncommitted change to a file Git already tracks
git stash list   # what's currently in the drawer
git stash pop    # put it back, and empty the drawer

body.p: One catch worth knowing now: a brand-new file Git has never seen stays exactly where it is. Untracked files — ones you've never `git add`ed — aren't swept into the drawer, because the stash only knows about files Git is already tracking.

body.tip: A stash isn't part of your project's history — it sits off to one side, attached to no branch, and it's easy to forget it's there. Git labels it for you (`WIP on main: ...`), and you can give it your own label with `git stash push -m "half-done nav bar"` — but a label is not a home. Treat the drawer as short-term storage: hours, not weeks. If a piece of work matters for longer than an afternoon, give it a commit on a branch instead, where it has a name and a place in the graph.

body.p: This is the private-notebook zone, and it's the only place where Git lets you genuinely rewrite the past. Two commands live here.
**`git commit --amend`** fixes the most recent commit — its message, its contents, or both. Stage whatever you forgot, then amend:

body.code:
git commit --amend -m "Add the contact page"    # fix a typo in the message

git add forgotten.txt
git commit --amend                              # fold a forgotten file into the last commit

body.tip: One difference between this sandbox and your own machine, worth knowing before it startles you. Real Git opens a text editor when you run `git commit --amend` without `-m` — and it does the same for `git revert`, which you'll meet in a few paragraphs — so that you can confirm the message it has written for you. Save and close the editor to let the command finish, or add `--no-edit` to accept the suggested message without opening anything. This sandbox skips the editor and goes straight through.

body.p: One detail matters more than it looks. **Amend does not edit a commit — it builds a brand-new one and points your branch at it instead.** You can watch this happen: the commit ID changes. The original commit is still sitting in storage, orphaned; your branch has stopped mentioning it.
That is exactly why amending something you've already pushed is trouble. Your teammate has the old commit; you now have a different one claiming to be the same piece of work.

**`git reset`** points your current branch at whatever commit you name. Usually that's an earlier one — which is why it feels like undoing, and why every commit after that point falls off the branch. But it can be any commit at all, including one your branch has already abandoned, and that's what makes the rescue at the end of this lesson possible. What happens to the *changes* those commits contained is decided by one of three flags — and this is the part worth learning properly, because the three do very different things:

list: `git reset --soft HEAD~1` — move the branch back one commit and leave everything **staged**. It feels as though you never pressed commit. This is the one for "I committed too early."

`git reset --mixed HEAD~1` — the default, so plain `git reset HEAD~1` means this. Move the branch back **and** unstage. Your files still hold every edit; you get to re-choose what goes into the next commit.
`git reset --hard HEAD~1` — move the branch back and **overwrite your files** with that older commit's version. Any uncommitted work in those files is destroyed.

body.p: A useful way to hold it: `--soft` touches only the branch pointer, `--mixed` touches the pointer and the staging area, `--hard` touches the pointer, the staging area, *and* your actual files.

body.warn: `--hard` is the only genuinely dangerous option in this module. Committed work it removes can nearly always be rescued with `git reflog` (below). Uncommitted work it removes cannot — that was never recorded anywhere. Make `git status` your reflex before typing `--hard`, so you know exactly what you're standing on.

body.h: What reset does to the picture

body.p: Here is a four-commit history. The newest commit added a contact page you now regret:

graph.caption: Before. main and HEAD both point at the newest commit, 'Add the contact page'.

body.p: Run `git reset --hard HEAD~1` and the history looks like this:

graph.caption: After git reset --hard HEAD~1. main and HEAD have stepped back one commit, and 'Add the contact page' is no longer drawn — nothing points at it any more. It still exists in Git's storage, which is what lets the reflog find it, but as far as your branch is concerned it never happened.

body.p: The commit wasn't so much deleted as *abandoned*. That's the shape to remember: **reset makes history shorter.**

Once you've pushed, `amend` and `reset` turn antisocial. Your teammate's clone still contains the commit you erased, so the next time either of you pushes or pulls, Git has to reconcile two histories that disagree about what happened. That is the classic way to ruin a Friday afternoon.

Concretely, your next `git push` comes back with the `! [rejected]` message from Module 7 — the remote is refusing to let you overwrite the version everyone else already has. If that happens to you, the way back is `git reset --hard origin/main`: it puts your branch exactly where the world thinks it is. Then undo the commit the public-safe way instead — which is what the rest of this lesson is about.

**`git revert <commit>`** is the public-safe undo. It looks at what that commit did and writes a **new commit that does the exact opposite** — deleting the file it added, putting back the line it removed. Nothing is rewritten. The mistake stays in the record, and so does the correction. Newspaper, then correction.

body.code:
git revert HEAD       # undo the most recent commit, with a new commit
git revert 0a53e15    # undo any commit at all, by its ID

body.p: Same starting history, same regret — but reverted instead of reset:

graph.caption: After git revert HEAD. Nothing was removed: 'Add the contact page' is still there, with a fifth commit sitting on top of it that undoes exactly what it did. Anyone who already pulled your history sees an addition, not a contradiction.

body.p: Reset makes history shorter; revert makes it **longer**. That single difference is the whole reason one is private-only and the other is safe to push.

body.tip: The decision, in one line: **if the commit has left your computer, revert it. If it hasn't, you're free to amend or reset it.**

body.p: Now the genuinely reassuring part. Git quietly records **every position `HEAD` has ever held** in your repository — every commit, every amend, every branch switch, every reset. This record is called the *reflog* (reference log). It lives only on your own machine, which is why most people never hear about it until the day it saves them. It isn't infinite, either — entries age out after a few months. The reflog is a rescue for this week's accident, not an archive.

body.analogy: `git log` is the official history — the story your project chooses to tell. `git reflog` is the security-camera footage: every move you actually made, in order, including the ones you'd rather nobody saw.

body.p: Suppose you amended a commit — changing its message from *Add the contact page* to *Add the contact form* — and then ran `git reset HEAD~2` to walk your branch two commits back. `git log` now shows a short, tidy history that's missing your work. `git reflog` shows this:

body.code:
$ git reflog
e442b84 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~2
f0fc65f HEAD@{1}: commit (amend): Add the contact form
caf962d HEAD@{2}: commit: Add the contact page
685ecb5 HEAD@{3}: commit: Add the pricing page
e442b84 HEAD@{4}: commit: Add the about page
2b437a4 HEAD@{5}: commit (initial): Add the homepage

body.p: Read it as a list of places HEAD has stood, newest at the top. Every line begins with a commit ID, and the `HEAD@{n}` handle beside it is how you name a position: `HEAD@{0}` is where you're standing now, `HEAD@{1}` is where you stood before that. You can see the whole story here: the amend at `HEAD@{1}` built `f0fc65f` to replace `caf962d` — which is why that line says *form* while `HEAD@{2}` still says *page* — and then the reset walked the branch back to `e442b84`.
`HEAD@{1}` is the commit you thought you'd destroyed — and now you have its ID. Point your branch back at it:

body.code: git reset --hard f0fc65f

body.p: ...and it's back, commits and files and all. That's the whole trick, and some version of it rescues almost any accident that involved a commit.

body.tip: Two habits cover nearly everything that can go wrong: run `git status` before you do anything destructive, and remember that `git reflog` exists **before** you panic, not after.

body.p: Reading about undo is one thing; doing it while nothing is at stake is what actually removes the fear. You're two chapters into a short story, and the second commit has a typo in its message. Over the next few commands you'll fix it, shelve some half-written work, take it back out, commit too early, un-commit, destroy the work on purpose — and then get it back.
Keep an eye on the commit graph and the commit IDs as you go. Watching an ID change is how you *see* that Git rewrites rather than edits.

Git didn't edit anything; it built a new commit and moved the branch onto it.

steps.say: Imagine someone now asks you to look at the file exactly as it was published, without your half-sentence in it. You don't want to commit an unfinished line, and you certainly don't want to delete it. Sweep it into the drawer instead.

expect.label: Working tree is clean — the edit is shelved, not lost

steps.say: Look at the file panel: chapter2.txt is back to its committed state, and `git status` would report nothing to commit. Nothing was lost. Tip the drawer back out.
Now commit it — deliberately a bit too early, so you have something to un-commit. Two commands: stage the file, then take the snapshot.

git add chapter2.txt
git commit -m "Finish chapter two"
steps.hint: git add chapter2.txt, then git commit -m "Finish chapter two"

expect.label: The new commit is called "Finish chapter two"

steps.say: Except the sentence still isn't finished — that commit was premature. `--soft` moves the branch back one commit and leaves every change **staged**, exactly as it was a second before you pressed commit. Check the file panel: your work is untouched, it's just no longer part of the history.
steps.hint: Type: git reset --soft HEAD~1 — HEAD~1 means "one commit before where I am".

expect.label: Your work is still staged, ready to re-commit

steps.say: Now do something reckless on purpose, in a sandbox where it costs you nothing: throw that work away. Two commands — take the change back out of the staging area, then overwrite the file with the committed version. (`git reset --hard HEAD` would have done both in one stroke; this is the same demolition in slow motion.) Read chapter2.txt afterwards — the sentence is gone.
steps.cmd:
git restore --staged chapter2.txt
git restore chapter2.txt
steps.hint: git restore --staged chapter2.txt, then git restore chapter2.txt

steps.say: That looks final. The commit is off the branch, the file has been overwritten, and `git log` shows no trace of either. But you *did* commit that work once, and Git quietly records every place HEAD has stood. Ask for the footage.

Find the line in your own reflog that reads `commit: Finish chapter two` and copy the code at the start of it — that's the commit you thought you'd destroyed. (If you typed everything exactly as shown, it will be `f17162e`.) Now point your branch straight back at it, and watch the commit — and the sentence in the file — come back together.
steps.hint: git reset --hard followed by the ID on the "commit: Finish chapter two" line of your reflog — `git reset --hard f17162e` if you followed along exactly.

expect.label: And your sentence came back with it

body.p: A trip-planning repo, and a genuinely bad afternoon. Two junk commits are sitting on the end of your history, and — much worse — a booking token was committed and **pushed** three commits ago. Two problems, on opposite sides of the shared line, so they need two different tools.
Run `git log --oneline` first. The `origin/main` label marks the last commit the world has seen: everything at or below it is newspaper, everything above it is private notebook.

setup.content:
Day 1: land in Lisbon.
Day 2: day trip to Sintra.

exercise.goal: Clean up both problems and leave a tidy, clean repository. (1) The two junk commits at the top — `wip` and `more wip` — were never pushed, so erase them from your history completely, taking `scratch.txt` with them. (2) The `Add booking details` commit **was** pushed, so its commit must stay in the history untouched — but `booking.txt` must no longer exist in your project. (3) `Add day two` is good work: `itinerary.txt` must still mention Sintra when you're done. Finish with a clean working tree, exactly five commits, and your cleaned-up history pushed — if you picked the right tool for the booking commit, `git push` will be accepted.
hints: Two problems, two tools. One of them lives above the origin/main line and one lives below it — re-read the two questions from the concept lesson and decide which tool each needs.

Deal with the junk commits first. They're the two newest, so one reset that moves the branch back two commits erases both — and if you pick the flavour that also rewrites your files, scratch.txt goes with them. Any other flavour leaves it sitting on disk for you to delete yourself.

With those gone, the booking commit is one step behind you. `git revert <commit>` writes a new commit that deletes what that one added — the original commit stays right where it is. Refs like HEAD~1 work here, and so does the ID from git log --oneline.
Overshot the reset and lost Sintra? That's exactly what git reflog is for: find the line for the 'Add day two' commit, copy its ID, and git reset --hard back onto it.

expect.label: scratch.txt is gone from your project
Exactly five commits: the two junk ones erased, one new one added
booking.txt is gone from your project
Your cleaned-up history is pushed — origin accepted it, so nothing it already had was rewritten

body.p: You never have to remember all of these at once. Answer the two questions — *has it been committed?* and *has it been shared?* — and only two or three of them are ever candidates.

list: **Not committed** — `git restore --staged <file>` un-stages and keeps your edit. `git restore <file>` discards the edit for good. `git stash` / `git stash pop` shelve work and bring it back.

**Committed, not shared** — `git commit --amend` replaces the last commit (new ID, so never amend something pushed). `git reset --soft` moves the branch and keeps everything staged; `--mixed` (the default) also unstages; `--hard` also overwrites your files.
**Shared** — `git revert <commit>` writes a new commit that undoes an old one. History gets longer, never rewritten, and everyone else stays in sync.
**When it all goes wrong** — `git reflog` lists every position HEAD has held. Find the ID of the commit you lost, then `git reset --hard <id>` to land back on it.

body.p: Reset makes history shorter, revert makes it longer. Here's the revert shape one more time — the mistake and its correction both on the record, which is exactly what you want when other people already have a copy:

graph.caption: A reverted mistake: the original commit stays, and a new commit on top undoes it.

body.p: One honest caveat: reverting a commit removes the file from your project going forward, but the old commit still contains it — which is fine for a bad idea and *not* fine for a leaked password. A secret that reaches a shared repository must be treated as compromised and rotated, no matter what you do to the history.
Next: `.gitignore` — how to keep the junk, the secrets and the giant generated files out of your history in the first place, so you need this module less often.

modules.title: .gitignore
modules.summary: What doesn't belong in a repository and how to keep it out: ignore patterns, the trap that catches everyone, and what to do when a secret is already committed.

body.p: Your project folder and your repository are not the same thing. The folder is everything sitting on your disk. The repository is what you have deliberately chosen to record. So far those have looked identical, because every file in these lessons was one you typed on purpose. Real projects are not like that.

Open a working project a few weeks old and you'll find hundreds of files nobody wrote by hand: downloaded libraries, compiled output, crash logs, a local database, a hidden file your editor left behind. Run `git status` in a folder like that and the useful information drowns.

body.analogy: Think of committing as packing for a house move. You box up the books, the photos, the furniture — the things that took effort and can't be replaced. You don't box the rubbish, and you don't box the contents of the fridge, because both regenerate wherever you land. And you certainly don't tape the front-door keys to the outside of a box you're about to ship across the country.

body.h: The four things that don't belong

list: **Dependencies and build output** — a *dependency* is code somebody else wrote that your project downloads in order to use; it lands in a folder like `node_modules/`. *Build output* is whatever your tools generate from your own source code — a `dist/` folder, a compiled program. Every one of these can be regenerated from the source you *did* commit. They're also enormous, and they change on every rebuild, so committing them buries your real history under thousands of diffs no human will ever read.

**Editor and operating-system junk** — `.DS_Store`, `.vscode/`, `.idea/`. These describe *your machine*, not the project. Your teammate uses a different editor, and you'd end up committing edits back and forth at each other forever.
**Logs and local databases** — `debug.log`, `dev.sqlite`. They grow every time you run the app. Yesterday's log output isn't part of the project any more than yesterday's weather is.

**Secrets** — API keys, passwords, tokens. An *API key* is a password your program uses to identify itself to another company's service — your payment processor, your email sender. Anyone holding it can spend money as you. A `.env` file (short for *environment*) is the usual place to keep those keys, which is why `.env` files are the classic thing to leak. This one isn't about tidiness. Everything above is a mess; this one is a bill, an outage, or a data breach.

body.tip: A useful test: *if I deleted this file and ran the project again, would it come back on its own?* If yes, it's output, and output doesn't get committed. Commit the recipe, not the cake.

body.p: Git's answer is a plain text file named `.gitignore`, living in the top folder of your project. One pattern per line. Lines starting with `#` are comments for humans. That's the whole format.

body.code:
# dependencies
node_modules/

# logs
*.log

# never commit this
secrets.env

body.p: Git reads that file before it shows you `git status` and before it stages anything. Any file matching a pattern becomes invisible: it stops appearing under "Untracked files", and `git add .` walks straight past it. The file is still there on your disk, working perfectly. Git has just stopped offering to record it.

list: `secrets.env` — an **exact name**. Matches files called exactly that. (In real Git that means one anywhere in the project, however deeply buried; this sandbox only looks in the top folder.)
`*.log` — an **extension**. The `*` means "anything", so this matches `debug.log`, `error.log`, and any other file ending in `.log`.
`node_modules/` — a **folder**. The trailing slash says "this is a directory": everything inside it, at any depth, is ignored.

body.tip: Real Git can do more — carve out exceptions to a rule, tie a rule to one particular folder, reach down through nested folders. The three shapes above cover the overwhelming majority of lines in real `.gitignore` files, and they're the three this sandbox understands, so they're the three we'll practise.

body.p: This surprises people: the file that says "don't commit things" is a file you commit. And it should be, because ignore rules are a decision about **the project**, not about you. Commit it, and every teammate who copies the repository gets the same rules automatically — nobody has to remember not to check in the build folder.

In practice `.gitignore` is usually one of the very first files in a new repository, written before the first commit. It is far cheaper to keep junk out than to get it back out later — which brings us to the rule that catches absolutely everyone.
**.gitignore only affects files Git isn't already tracking.**

Once a file has been in a commit, Git is tracking it. Adding its name to `.gitignore` afterwards does precisely nothing: `git status` keeps reporting its changes, `git add .` keeps staging them, and the file keeps riding along in every snapshot. Beginners write the rule, see no change, and assume they got the pattern wrong. The pattern was fine. The file was already inside.

body.analogy: An ignore rule is a bouncer on the door, not a security guard inside the club. It can stop a file getting in. It has no authority whatsoever over the ones already sitting at the bar.

body.p: To stop tracking something you've already committed, you have to remove it from the project and commit that removal. From the moment it's gone, it's untracked again, and *now* the ignore rule applies to it — so when the build tool recreates that folder tomorrow, Git says nothing.

body.warn: Removing a file from your project deletes it from your folder too. For build output that's harmless — it regenerates. For a real `secrets.env` you actually need, copy it somewhere safe first. (Outside this sandbox, real Git has `git rm --cached <file>`, which unhooks a file from tracking while leaving your copy on disk. This simulator doesn't implement it, so we'll use plain `rm` on files we can afford to lose.)

body.h: Adding an ignored file on purpose

body.p: Try to stage an ignored file and Git stops you, and tells you how to insist:

body.code:
git add secrets.env
# The following paths are ignored by one of your .gitignore files:
# secrets.env
# hint: Use -f if you really want to add them.

body.p: `git add -f secrets.env` overrides the rule for that one file (`-f` for *force*). It is not a workaround to reach for casually — but it has honest uses. The classic one: your rule is `*.env`, and you want to commit an `example.env` full of fake placeholder values, so new teammates know which settings they need to fill in. The rule is right; this one file is the deliberate exception.

body.warn: If you ever type `git add -f` on a file with a real password in it, stop and ask what you're doing. The refusal you're overriding is the one piece of protection Git offers here.

body.h: When the secret is already committed

body.p: Here is the honest, uncomfortable part. You committed `config.env` with a live payment key in it three weeks ago. Today you notice, wipe the key out of the file, add it to `.gitignore`, and commit. Your working folder is clean. Are you safe?
No. Deleting a file changes the *newest* snapshot. It cannot change the old ones — that permanence is the entire point of a commit, and it doesn't switch off for embarrassing commits.

graph.caption: Three commits. The key went in with the first one and is still sitting inside it, in full. The third commit blanked out `config.env` and added a `.gitignore` — and changed nothing whatsoever about the first, or about the copy of this history anyone else already has.

body.p: And if you ever pushed that history to a shared server, assume it has been copied — by teammates, by backups, by automated scanners that trawl public repositories for exactly this. So the real-world response, in this order:

list: **Rotate the credential. First. Today.** Revoke the key, change the password, issue a new token. This is the only step that actually makes you safe, and it works no matter who already has the old history.

**Then scrub the history**, if the repo is shared or public. This needs specialist tooling — `git filter-repo` or the BFG Repo-Cleaner — which rewrites every affected commit and requires everyone on the team to re-sync. It's disruptive, and it is not something you improvise at 2am.
**Then add the ignore rule**, so the same file can't wander back in next week.

body.warn: Rotate before you scrub. A beautifully cleaned history whose key is still live is worse than doing nothing, because it *feels* solved. The key is compromised the moment it's pushed; only revoking it changes that.

body.tip: All of which is an argument for the cheapest version of this whole module: write `.gitignore` before your first commit. Ten seconds at the start, versus a very bad afternoon later.

body.p: You've inherited a small web project. It has one commit of real work in it — and, since you last ran it, a pile of files you never wrote: downloaded libraries, log files, and a `secrets.env` file holding a live API key. You're going to teach Git to look away from all of it, then deal with a piece of junk that a previous developer already committed.

setup.content:
# Corner Shop
A very small web shop.
generated by the build tool at 11:58 - do not edit

console.log('Welcome to the shop');
console.log('Now with free delivery');

steps.say: Start where you always start, and count what Git is showing you: one real edit to `app.js` that you care about, buried under five untracked files you never wrote — two logs, two downloaded libraries and a live API key. This is what a real project looks like without ignore rules.
Before you hide `secrets.env`, look at what's actually in it. That is a live payment key. If you ran `git add .` right now, it would go into your next snapshot — and into history permanently.
Create the ignore file. `.gitignore` is an ordinary text file, so you make it the ordinary way. The first pattern is an **exact name** — it matches this one file and nothing else.

Now the other two shapes. Note the double arrow: `>>` **appends** a line, where the single `>` you used a moment ago *replaces* the whole file — using it here would wipe out the line you just wrote. `*.log` catches every log file, present and future; `node_modules/` catches an entire folder.

Look again. The logs, the libraries and the key have vanished from the listing — three patterns silenced five files. What's left is the truth about your project: one edit, plus the new `.gitignore` waiting to be committed.

Test the guard rail: try to stage the key deliberately. Git refuses and tells you about `-f` — read that message, it's the one that saves you one day. Then stage everything with `git add .` and notice it quietly skips the ignored files.
steps.hint: Run git add secrets.env (it will refuse — that's the point), then git add .

expect.label: secrets.env stayed out of the staging area

steps.say: Commit. Read the stat block: **two files changed**. The rules themselves are now part of the project's history, so anyone who copies this repository inherits them without being told.
steps.cmd: git commit -m "Add .gitignore and update the welcome message"
steps.hint: git commit -m "Add .gitignore and update the welcome message"

expect.label: The commit contains nothing but .gitignore and app.js

steps.say: Now the trap. `build/bundle.js` is generated output that a previous developer committed by mistake, so Git is already tracking it. Add a `build/` rule, then pretend the build tool runs and rewrites the bundle — the text doesn't matter, only that the file changed — and look at the status. It's **still** listed as modified. The rule changed nothing, because the file was already inside.
steps.cmd:
echo "build/" >> .gitignore
echo "rebuilt at 12:09" > build/bundle.js
git status
steps.hint: Append build/ to .gitignore, overwrite build/bundle.js with any text at all, then run git status.

expect.label: See that build/bundle.js is still reported

steps.say: The only cure is to stop tracking it: remove the file from the project and commit that removal. It's build output, so losing the copy costs nothing — it regenerates. From this commit onward `build/` is untracked, the rule finally bites, and Git will never mention the bundle again.
steps.cmd:
rm build/bundle.js
git add .
git commit -m "Stop tracking generated build output"
steps.hint: rm build/bundle.js, then git add . (this stages the deletion), then commit it.

expect.label: build/bundle.js is out of the project
The commit records the removal and the new rule

body.p: A repository in a genuinely bad state. Somebody committed `deploy.env` — with a live AWS secret key in it — back in the first commit. Since then the app has been run a few times, leaving logs and a `cache/` folder scattered around. There's also `example.env`: a placeholder listing the settings a new teammate has to fill in, with nothing real in it. And you've just improved the README, which is worth keeping.

Clean the house. The checklist watches the *state* of the repo, so any route that gets there counts. Two things it will hold you to. The junk has to still be sitting on your disk when you're done — ignoring is not deleting. And `example.env` has to end up committed, even though the rule you're about to write covers it: that file is the deliberate exception, and Git will make you say so out loud.

body.warn: Two things before you start. First: in real life you would have revoked that AWS key this morning, before touching Git at all — and taken a copy of anything you still needed. Assume you've done both; this exercise is the tidying that comes afterwards. Second: when your checklist is green, run `git show HEAD~1` and read the output. The key is still there, in full, and always will be. Removing a file changes the newest snapshot, never the old ones.

setup.content:
# Booking App

Run it with `node index.js`. Ask a teammate for the deployment credentials.

exercise.goal: End with `git status` completely silent — nothing modified, nothing staged, and nothing untracked — while `build.log`, `test.log` and the `cache/` files are all still sitting in your project folder. Your committed `.gitignore` must ignore the `cache/` folder, every `.log` file and every `.env` file. `deploy.env` itself must be gone from the project, so Git stops tracking it — while `example.env` ends up committed anyway, as a deliberate exception to your own rule. Do the whole cleanup in a single new commit on top of the initial one, carrying those changes and your README improvement and nothing else.
hints: Three rules, and you only need two of the three shapes: a folder pattern ends with a slash, an extension pattern starts with a star and a dot. One extension rule can cover both `.env` files at once. Build the file up with echo "..." > .gitignore and then echo "..." >> .gitignore.

Adding an env rule will NOT make Git stop tracking deploy.env — it was in the first commit, so it's already inside. Get it out of the project, and stage that removal like any other change. Leave the logs and the cache exactly where they are: the point is that Git can't see them, not that they're gone.

git add . stages new files, edits and deletions all at once — and walks straight past anything your .gitignore covers, which now includes example.env. Try staging that one by name and read what Git says: this is the one time you mean to override the refusal.

The finishing sequence: git add -f example.env to force in the exception, then — there is no git rm in this sandbox — the shell's rm deploy.env, then git add . to stage that deletion alongside your new .gitignore and the README edit, then one git commit -m "...".

expect.label: A committed .gitignore hides the cache/ folder
deploy.env is gone from your project folder
example.env is committed anyway — the deliberate exception
git status is completely silent — nothing modified, nothing untracked
build.log is still on disk — Git just can't see it
...and the cache folder is still there too
One cleanup commit: the rules, the README, the removal and the exception — and no junk riding along

list: A repository holds the **source of truth**, not everything in the folder. Dependencies, build output, editor junk, logs and secrets stay out.
`.gitignore` is plain text, one pattern per line, `#` for comments — and it is **committed**, so the whole team shares the rules.
Three pattern shapes: `secrets.env` (exact name), `*.log` (extension), `node_modules/` (whole folder).
**Ignore rules only apply to untracked files.** Already committed? The rule does nothing until you remove the file from the project and commit that removal.
`git add <ignored file>` is refused; `git add -f <file>` overrides it, for deliberate exceptions like an `example.env` full of fake values.
A committed secret is not fixed by deleting it — old commits still hold it. **Rotate the credential first**, then scrub history with a specialist tool, then add the rule.

graph.caption: The cheap version of this whole module: .gitignore lands in the very first commit. Every log file and downloaded library that appears afterwards is invisible from birth, and the history stays a record of decisions rather than a record of build runs.

body.p: Next, the last module: commit hygiene — what makes a commit message worth reading, how to keep each commit to one idea, and how to fix the message you just got wrong.

modules.title: Commit Hygiene
modules.summary: The finale: writing messages a stranger could follow, sizing each commit so it says one thing, and fixing the last commit when you get it wrong.

lessons.title: Messages your future self will love

body.p: It's eleven at night. Something about pricing is broken, and you've narrowed it down to one of the last few commits. You open the log to find the one that touched the cart. Here is what you find:

body.code:
a1c9f0e  fix
7b2d114  more stuff
0e91a22  asdf
c4471be  final FINAL v2
9d0aa31  fix again

body.p: Not one of these tells you anything. The person who wrote them knew exactly what each one meant — for about four hours. That person was you.

Every command in this course has been about *recording* your work. This last module is about the other half of the job: making the record **readable**. A history nobody can read is only slightly better than no history at all.

body.h: A commit message is a letter to a stranger

body.analogy: Think about labelling boxes when you move house. You are not labelling them for the person packing — that person can see what's going in. You are labelling them for the person unpacking: tired, in an unfamiliar room, at midnight, holding a box that says **stuff**. A commit message is that label. The person unpacking is almost always you.

body.p: So here's the test to hold every message against: *would this make sense to someone who wasn't there, reading it two years from now, with no memory of the afternoon I wrote it?* If yes, it's a good message. If it only makes sense because you remember the context, it isn't — because the context is exactly the thing that evaporates.

A full Git commit message has three parts, and the shape is the same everywhere in the Git world. Don't worry if the subject matter of the example is unfamiliar — you're looking at the shape, not the security. Notice where the line breaks fall, and what each part is for:

body.code:
Add rate limiting to the login endpoint

Repeated failed logins let an attacker try passwords all night.
Five attempts per minute per IP stops that without getting in
the way of a real person who fumbled their password twice.

We rate-limit per IP rather than per account on purpose: locking
accounts by name is itself an attack, because anyone who knows
your username could lock you out.

list: The **subject line** — one short line, around 50 characters, no full stop at the end. This is the part everyone actually reads, and often the only part they see.
A **blank line** — not decoration. It is how Git tells the subject from the body; every tool that shows you "just the summary" cuts exactly there.

The **body** — as many lines as you need, explaining **why**. Break the lines yourself at around 72 characters; Git won't wrap them for you, and an unwrapped paragraph turns into one enormous line in half the tools that display it.

body.tip: How do you actually *type* that blank line? Repeat the flag. `git commit -m "Add rate limiting" -m "Traffic tripled after launch and the login endpoint was the first thing to buckle."` — Git joins each `-m` with a blank line between them, so the first becomes your subject and the rest become the body. That works here and on your own machine. (Running `git commit` with no `-m` at all is the other way: real Git opens a text editor for you.)
Small, obvious changes don't need a body at all. `Fix typo in README` is a complete and excellent commit message. Save your words for the changes that will confuse somebody.

body.h: Write the subject as a command

body.p: Git's own convention is the **imperative mood** — write the subject as an instruction to the codebase. "Add rate limiting," not "Added rate limiting," not "Adding rate limiting," and definitely not "rate limiting stuff."

body.tip: The sentence trick: a good subject finishes the sentence *"If applied, this commit will ______."* — "If applied, this commit will **add rate limiting to the login endpoint**." That reads right. "If applied, this commit will **fixed the thing**" does not. If the sentence sounds wrong, the subject is wrong.

body.p: Why bother with the mood? Because Git writes messages too, and it writes them that way: `Merge branch 'feature'`, `Revert "Add rate limiting"`. Yours will sit in the same list. When every line is phrased the same way, you can read a hundred of them without changing gears.

body.code:
✗  fix
✗  update stuff
✗  asdf
✗  final FINAL v2
✗  changes as discussed
✗  Fixed the bug where the cart total came out wrong for items on
   sale because the discount was applied after tax instead of before

✓  Fix cart total for discounted items
✓  Remove the legacy CSV importer
✓  Add rate limiting to the login endpoint
✓  Rename getUsr to getUser throughout

body.p: The first five say nothing. The sixth is the opposite problem, and it's worth looking at closely: it isn't wrong, it's **misfiled**. "Fix cart total for discounted items" is the subject; everything after "because" is body material. Splitting it across a blank line costs nothing and makes both halves readable.

body.h: The body explains WHY. The diff already shows what.

body.p: The single most common mistake in a commit body is narrating the diff: "changed line 40 of cart.js, added an if statement." Git can already show you that, perfectly, forever — `git show` prints the exact change. Spending your body on it is like captioning a photo with a list of the objects in the photo.
The body is for the things the diff can never tell anyone:

list: Why the change was needed at all — the bug report, the complaint, the thing that broke.
What you tried first that didn't work, so nobody re-tries it in a year.
The constraint that forced an odd-looking choice.
What you deliberately left out, and why.
Anything that will look like a mistake to a future reader and isn't.

body.h: Half of a good message is choosing what goes in the commit

body.p: You cannot write a one-line summary of a commit that does five unrelated things. If your subject line needs the word **and**, that is usually not a writing problem — it is a commit problem. "Fix the cart total and rename the button and update the readme" is three commits wearing one coat.
An **atomic commit** is one logical change: about one thing, and complete on its own.

body.analogy: A commit is a **paragraph**. Not a word — a commit that adjusts one space in a comment is noise in the log. Not a chapter — a commit that rewrites half the app can't be read, can't be reviewed, and can't be undone without collateral damage. One idea, stated completely, then a break.

body.p: Note that "one thing" is not the same as "one file." Adding a login page might touch `login.html`, `login.css` and a line of routing code — that's still one logical change, and it belongs in one commit. Meanwhile a single file can easily contain two unrelated edits that belong in two.
Here is why the size matters, concretely. Suppose three weeks of work went in like this:

graph.caption: Three weeks of work in a single commit — the one on the right. One commit is one handle: if any part of that work turns out to be wrong, your only undo button removes all of it.

body.p: Now the same three weeks, committed as the work actually happened:

graph.caption: The same work, committed one piece at a time. Six handles instead of one: revert the commit that broke checkout and every other change survives. Hover a dot to read its message — this log is a changelog you never had to write.

ops.message: Add a cart that remembers its items
Show a running total in the cart
Style the shop for narrow screens
Document how to run the shop locally

body.p: Same code, same three weeks, wildly different repository. The second one gives you a surgical `git revert`, a history you can skim, and changes small enough that a reviewer actually reads them. A forty-line commit gets read. A four-thousand-line commit gets "looks good to me."

body.h: git commit --amend: the eraser for the last thing you said

body.p: You already met `git commit --amend` in Module 9, where it was an undo tool — the thing you reach for when the last commit is wrong. It is the same command here, doing a different job: it is the eraser for the message you just wrote. You press Enter, and half a second later you spot the typo in your own subject line. Or you notice the commit is missing a file that plainly belongs with it.

body.code:
# with nothing staged, this changes only the message:
git commit --amend -m "Fix cart total for discounted items"

# fold in a file you forgot, keeping the message untouched:
git add login.css
git commit --amend --no-edit

body.tip: `--no-edit` means "keep the old message, don't ask me about it". Leave it off and real Git opens your text editor with the old message already filled in — you'd save and close to keep it unchanged. That editor is the same one from the tip further up, and it's where you'd type the blank line and body. The terminal here has no editor, so it keeps the message either way; get into the habit of writing `--no-edit`, because that is the form that behaves identically everywhere.

body.p: One trap worth naming: `--amend` always rebuilds the newest commit out of **whatever is staged at that moment**, `-m` or no `-m`. Anything sitting in the staging area gets swept in, even when you thought you were only relabelling. Run `git status` before you amend, the same way you would before any commit.

The rest is Module 9's lesson, unchanged: "amend" is a polite word for **replace**. Git builds a brand-new commit with the same parent and the corrected contents, then moves your branch onto it — which is why the ID changes, why the old commit is still sitting in `git reflog`, and why this rule still stands:

body.warn: Amend only commits you have **not** pushed. Once a commit is on a remote, other people's history contains it, and replacing it means your history and theirs now disagree about what happened. You find out the hard way: your next `git push` is rejected as non-fast-forward, and Git's hint suggests `git pull` — the one time in this course that advice is wrong, because pulling merges the old commit straight back in and you end up with **both** copies of it in your history. There is an escape hatch (`git push --force-with-lease`), and needing it under pressure is precisely the bad afternoon this rule exists to save you from. Rewrite freely before you push, never after.

body.tip: `--amend` reaches exactly one commit — the tip of your current branch. It cannot fix the message three commits back. Which is one more reason to write it properly the first time.

body.p: Notice that this lesson introduced no new commands at all. Hygiene isn't a feature you switch on; it's the judgement of when to press the shutter and what to write underneath. You already have every tool you need.

You're back on Corner Shop, a tiny online shop you worked on last week. Past-you left a commit called `stuff`, and present-you has two unrelated edits sitting in the working directory. Let's clean up behind past-you and then do it properly going forward — and before you worry: this repo has never been pushed anywhere. Nobody else has these commits, so rewriting them is completely safe. That's the condition the warning in the last lesson was about, and here it's satisfied.

body.p: The last challenge of the course. You've come back to a small project called Bookclub after a few days away, and there's a mess to turn into a history you'd be happy for someone else to read. Three jobs:

list: The newest commit, `Add a login form`, is incomplete: `login.css` belongs in it but was never staged. Fold that file into **that** commit and leave its message alone — no separate "forgot a file" commit.
The edit in `app.js` (an empty password is now rejected) is a bug fix. Give it a commit of its own.
The edits in `README.md` and `docs/setup.md` are one documentation change spread across two files. They go together, in a single final commit.

body.p: There's a trap in here, and it's a fair one: one of those three jobs can only be done first. Work out which one before you type anything.

hints: Think about order first. `git commit --amend` only ever reaches the commit at the very tip of your branch — so which of the three jobs is impossible once you've committed anything on top?

To complete an existing commit: stage the missing file with `git add login.css`, then run `git commit --amend --no-edit`. That rebuilds the tip commit with the extra file and leaves its message alone.

"One logical change" is not "one file." You can stage several at once: `git add README.md docs/setup.md`, then make a single commit. Check yourself before you call it done, with `git log --oneline` and `git status`: four commits, nothing modified, nothing untracked. If a subject line needs the word "and", you've merged two commits that should have stayed apart.

Committed too soon and buried the login commit? You are not stuck. `git reset HEAD~1` from Module 9 lifts the newest commit off the branch and leaves its changes in your working directory, **unstaged** — so your next `git add` picks up only the file you name, and nothing can sneak into the amend. Run it once for each commit you need to lift, then start again from the amend.

The login commit now carries both of its files
The bug fix has a commit to itself
One documentation commit covering both docs files
The last commit's message is a real subject line, not "docs" or "wip"

list: A commit message is a letter to a stranger who has forgotten everything — and that stranger is usually **you**, two years from now.
Shape: a **subject line** of about 50 characters, a **blank line**, then a body. The blank line is what separates them for every tool that reads Git.
Write the subject in the **imperative**, so it finishes *"If applied, this commit will ______."*
The body explains **why**. Never narrate the diff — `git show` already does that better than you can.
An **atomic commit** is one logical change, complete on its own. One thing, not one file.
The "and" smell: if your subject needs the word *and*, you probably need two commits.
`git commit --amend` fixes the newest commit — `-m "..."` for a new message, or stage a file first and `--amend --no-edit` to fold it in without touching the message.
Amending **replaces** a commit rather than editing it. Rewrite freely before you push; never after.

body.p: Eleven modules ago, a folder was just a folder and the only way to keep an old version of anything was to name a file `final_FINAL_v2`. Look at what you can do now.

list: **Record work**: `init`, `status`, `add`, `commit`, and the staging area that lets you choose what goes in each snapshot.
**Read a repository**: `log`, `diff`, `diff --staged`, `show` — you can walk into any project and find out what happened and when.
**Work in parallel**: branches as movable pointers, `switch -c`, `merge`, and the confidence to sit down and resolve a conflict instead of panicking.
**Work with other people**: remotes, `push`, `fetch`, `pull`, and the feature-branch workflow that nearly every software team on earth runs on.
**Undo almost anything**: `restore`, `reset`, `revert`, `stash`, `reflog` — and the knowledge of which of those are safe to use on shared history.
**Keep it clean**: `.gitignore`, atomic commits, and messages people thank you for.

body.p: Here's the part worth holding on to: there is no second, harder Git hiding behind this one. Everything you haven't met yet is built out of the same few pieces you already understand. A tag is a name pinned to a commit. Cherry-picking is replaying one commit somewhere else. Rebasing is re-writing a chain of commits onto a different parent. A pull request is a branch, plus a conversation. Every one of those is a way of moving around on the graph you've been watching redraw itself all course.

list: **Use it today, on something real.** Take any folder you care about — notes, a spreadsheet-free budget, a half-finished website — and run `git init`. Ten small commits on a real project will teach you more than another ten lessons.

**Push something to a remote.** Make an account on a hosting service, create an empty repository, and connect it with the `git remote add` and `git push -u` you learned in Module 7. Seeing your own history appear on a web page makes it click.
**Read someone else's log.** Clone a project you admire and run `git log --oneline`. You'll spot the good messages and the bad ones immediately now, which is proof you learned something.
**Let Git teach you the rest.** `git help <command>` and `git <command> --help` describe every flag of every command, and now you have the vocabulary to read them.
**Come back to the playground** any time you want to try something frightening before you try it for real. Nothing here can break.

body.p: The habit that matters most is the smallest one: commit often, and say what you did. Everything else in Git exists to reward you for that. Go make something worth keeping a history of.
